The overall increase of $804,000 for the 9 special political missions is attributable primarily to increased requirements for civilian personnel resulting from the application of lower vacancy rates and the application of the latest salary rates. The increase was offset in part by reduced requirements: (a) resulting from the proposed net abolishment of 89 posts and positions, especially in UNAMA and BINUH; (b) the reduction of the BINUH’s civilian personnel complement due to the handover of support functions to UNSOH and its revised mandate; (c) reduced rental and maintenance costs for the  premises in Tripoli based on latest contractual arrangement, as well as well as non-recurrent provision for security construction approved in 2026 in UNSMIL; (d) reduced requirements under air operations owing to the downsizing of the mission’s fleet by two aircraft in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia, and a reduction in flight hours based on the latest utilization rates in UNSMIL and UNAMA; (e) lower communication carrier and connectivity costs, as well as reduced centralized services costs, resulting from efficiency measures taken since 2025 that included the lower staffing levels and the closure of 10 sub-regional offices in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia; (f) reduced requirements for fuel for generators reflecting energy-efficiency measures and a reduced mission footprint following the closure and nationalization of field offices approved in 2026 in UNAMA; and (e) reduced requirements for military and police personnel resulting from the reconfiguration of deployments, including the decrease in the actual deployed strength of United Nations Guard Unit in UNSMIL 167 out of 234 authorized personnel and the decrease in the deployment of United Nations police officers in BINUH from 48 to 5 personnel.
Vacancy rates

The proposed vacancy rates applied in the budget take into account the experience to date. The assumptions considered for the proposed vacancy factors include: (a) the 12-month average vacancy rate from January to December in 2025; and (b) the actual vacancy rate as at 31 March 2026. The lower of the two was used as the budgeted vacancy rate.

For BINUH and UNAMA where there are a large number of posts proposed for abolishment in 2027, the proposed vacancy rates duly considered the total number of vacant posts and positions as of 31 March 2026, net of the number of posts and positions proposed for abolishment, so as to arrive at the appropriate budgeted vacancy rates.

The above approach is in line with the policy guidance to improve the accuracy and consistency of the vacancy factors applied in the proposed budgets for 2027 and to ensure that the proposed vacancy rates are based, as much as possible, on actual rates. A vacancy rate of 50 per cent has been applied when calculating the costs associated with proposed establishments and reassignments. Annex II outlines the proposed vacancy rates for 2027.
Efficiency gains

The proposed budget reflects efficiency and cost‑reduction measures, resulting in reduced requirements for military and police personnel, civilian personnel and operational costs. Requirements for military and police personnel are reduced primarily as a result of the planned utilization of commercial airlines, in lieu of charter flights, for the rotation of the United Nations Guard Unit personnel in UNSMIL. Requirements for civilian personnel are reduced mainly as a result of: (a) the proposed abolition of 61 posts and the downward reclassification of two posts (1 P‑5 and 1 P‑4) in UNAMA, reflecting targeted efficiency measures through organizational optimization, functional streamlining and improved resource allocation; (b) the proposed abolition of one D‑1 post and the nationalization of two international posts (1 P‑3 and 1 P‑2) to National Professional Officers in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia; and (c) the promotion of national capacity for the delivery of critical mandated activities in UNSMIL.
In addition, requirements for operational costs are reduced mainly owing to efficiencies achieved under the following classes of expenditure:

(a) facilities and infrastructure, reflecting reduced fuel consumption for generators resulting from project upgrades in UNAMA; and fuel‑optimization measures, including reduced heating in non‑essential areas and the use of smaller generators after working hours for critical facilities only, leading to a reduction in fuel consumption from 36,000 litres in 2026 to 25,000 litres in 2027 in UNSCOL;
(b) consultants and consulting services, owing to increased reliance on in‑house capacity in UNOWAS;

(c) ground transportation, reflecting reduced projected fuel consumption in UNOWAS, following a review of actual utilization patterns; as well as the transfer of vehicles (four light vehicle patrols and two armoured vehicles) from the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) to UNSCOL, eliminating planned procurement;

(d) air operations, reflecting the discontinuation of the rental and operation of fixed‑wing aircraft and the consolidation of aviation requirements in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia; the establishment of a cost‑recovery arrangement for the use of air assets of the United Nations Support Office in Haiti (UNSOH) in lieu of a separate aviation contract in BINUH; and the use of commercial airlines in UNOCA in lieu of the use of special flights associated with its previous co-shared fixed-wing aircraft with the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo;

(e) communications and information technology, reflecting the transfer of equipment and supplies, including computers and accessories, from UNIFIL to UNSCOL through asset optimization and improved operational practices, replacing end‑of‑life assets and eliminating planned procurement; as well as reduced staffing levels, revised Office of Information and Communications Technology guidelines and a reduction in the number of radio base stations from 15 to 11 in UNAMA;

(f) medical services, reflecting a change in modality for paramedic services from commercial contracts to individual contractors in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia; and a reduction in the size of the critical care team in UNAMA in line with revised contractual arrangements and operating modalities; and

(g) other supplies, services and equipment, reflecting the transfer of supplies, including rations, from UNIFIL to UNSCOL; reduced freight volumes resulting from lower acquisition requirements and reduced unit costs for rations following a change in ration types in UNAMA.

Missions achieved efficiencies and savings during the performance period in 2025 through a variety of measures, including: (a) in UNSMIL, revised contractual arrangements and cost reductions for the sustainment of the Mission’s compound in Tripoli following the relocation of staff from Tripoli to Tunisia; (b) in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia, the conduct of a cost‑benefit analysis resulting in the adoption of the United Nations Fleet lease arrangement as a more efficient and cost‑effective modality than commercial contracts, leveraging shared United Nations fleet services, as well as the extension of tours of duty for military observers, resulting in reduced travel costs; and (c) in UNAMA, the abolishment of 17 driver posts following further streamlining of activities, the abolishment of one post of Chief, Supply Chain Management (P‑5), in connection with the consolidation of the Supply Chain Management and Service Delivery Management pillars, drawing on experience gained in UNAMI, the restructuring of personnel associated with the proposed partial outsourcing of staff counsellor services, as well as further efficiencies achieved through a revised security posture, revised contractual arrangements for rent and camp management services, and the redesign of the delivery of mine action mandates.

children.text: Extrabudgetary resources
For the sake of brevity, the present document will include a section on extrabudgetary resources only for those missions that have projected extrabudgetary resources in 2026 or 2027.
Gender perspective

Special political missions are guided by Security Council resolutions on women and peace and security agenda and mandate the incorporation of a gender perspective into the political work of the United Nations, including in special political missions. The missions are also guided by General Assembly resolution 75/100 on the comprehensive review of special political missions, in which the Assembly reaffirmed the important role of women in the prevention and resolution of conflicts and in peacebuilding and recognised the importance of the equal and effective participation and the full involvement of women at all levels, at all stages and in all aspects of the peaceful settlement of disputes, conflict prevention and conflict resolution.

Specific examples of how special political missions integrate a gender perspective into their operational activities, deliverables and results are given under the individual missions in the present report.
Disability inclusion

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, special political missions review the Strategy with a view to further advancing disability inclusion through inclusive messaging, awareness-raising and promoting the Strategy through their work, including in political and peace processes. The missions also support mitigating measures to overcome accessibility challenges, in addition to the efforts undertaken by relevant United Nations entities to ensure the accessibility of facilities, platforms, security and other infrastructure to facilitate easy access and use by persons with disabilities.
Evaluation activities

In 2025, the Office of Internal Oversight Services completed its biennial assessment on strengthening the role of evaluation and the application of evaluation findings on programme design, delivery and policy directives. Mission-specific evaluation activities are described, as applicable, under the specific missions in the present report.
Special political missions
1.	United Nations Office for West Africa and the Sahel
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The United Nations Office for West Africa and the Sahel (UNOWAS) is responsible for conflict prevention and ensuring sustainable peace and security in West Africa and the Sahel. Its mandate derives from the exchanges of letters between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council (S/2016/88 and S/2016/89, S/2016/1128 and S/2016/1129, S/2019/1009 and S/2020/85, S/2023/70 and S/2023/71 and S/2026/53 and S/2026/83), as well as Council resolution 2349 (2017). The mission’s current mandate will expire on 31 January 2029.

UNOWAS is mandated to: (a) monitor political developments in West Africa and the Sahel and carry out good offices to support conflict prevention, peacebuilding, sustaining peace and mediation efforts in the subregion, mindful of the sustainable development context; (b) enhance regional and subregional partnerships to address cross-border and cross-cutting threats to peace and security; (c) support, through political advocacy and playing a convening role, the implementation of the United Nations integrated strategy for the Sahel; and (d) promote good governance, respect for the rule of law, human rights, constitutional order and women, peace and security considerations in conflict prevention, management and resolution initiatives in West Africa and the Sahel.

In 2026, an independent review on the mandate and activities of UNOWAS will be conducted as per the exchange of letters between the Secretary-General and the Security Council (S/2026/53 and S/2026/83).
Programme of work
Objective
The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to achieve peace and security in West Africa and the Sahel.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

Strengthen its early warning and conflict prevention and resolution action with relevant partners, with a focus on West African countries undergoing political transitions and those scheduled to hold elections in 2027; de-escalate crises relating to governance challenges; lead regional and international diplomatic engagements to build consensus on regional responses; support regional solutions to cross-cutting threats to peace and security; and monitor and assess political developments in the region;

Enhance partnerships with regional and subregional institutions, civil society organizations and United Nations entities to address regional peace and security challenges, focusing on root causes of instability and insecurity in the region, while reinforcing the peace-security-development nexus; and conduct high-level advocacy to facilitate humanitarian assistance and access to critical social services by populations affected by conflict and insecurity;

Accelerate the implementation of the women, peace and security and youth, peace and security agendas through the promotion of involvement of women and young people in political and decision-making processes and mediation initiatives; and advance the promotion of good governance and respect for human rights and the rule of law;
Strengthen its analytical work, including on governance, constitutional order, and the adverse implications of climate change.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Prevention and mitigation of conflicts through consultative political processes, including in countries undergoing political transitions;

Strengthened regional and subregional cross-border responses and coherent, comprehensive and integrated approaches to challenges relating to climate change, transnational organized crime, illicit trafficking, farmer and herder dynamics, intercommunal violence, terrorism, violent extremism and humanitarian access;
Mainstreaming of women and youth participation into conflict prevention, management and resolution activities;
Strengthened initiatives to address violations of human rights and international humanitarian law and improve constitutional order and security sector governance.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, UNOWAS works with the African Union, the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), the Mano River Union, the Lake Chad Basin Commission Initiative, the Liptako-Gourma Authority, the Gulf of Guinea Commission, the African Development Bank and other regional entities, national human rights institutions and other civil society groups in the region. The mission’s cooperation with these entities aim to strengthen and harmonize regional capacities for conflict prevention and resolution, peacebuilding; advance good governance, constitutional order and respect for human rights and the rule of law and the participation of women and young people in political and decision-making processes; and support regional responses to address climate change as well as cross-border threats to peace and security.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, UNOWAS collaborates with the Development Coordination Office and resident coordinators, humanitarian coordinators, United Nations country teams, United Nations agencies, funds and programmes based in Dakar and across the region and other United Nations partners to create political space for humanitarian access and developmental initiatives, including the United Nations integrated strategy for the Sahel. It coordinates with the United Nations Regional Office for Central Africa (UNOCA) on transregional issues affecting West and Central Africa, including terrorism in the Lake Chad Basin, farmer-herder conflicts, climate security, piracy and maritime security in the Gulf of Guinea.
In relation to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
Demand for UNOWAS good offices to facilitate political dialogue and defuse political tensions, and to support countries undergoing political transitions and institutional reforms;

Heads of State and Governments of West Africa, ECOWAS, the Lake Chad Basin Commission, the Mano River Union, the African Union, the Gulf of Guinea Commission and other regional entities demonstrate the political will for sustained support to regional peace and security mechanisms and a commitment to mobilizing the resources required to address challenges to peace and stability;
ECOWAS early warning and response mechanisms and other regional conflict prevention instruments are operational at the national and regional levels;
The international community remains committed to supporting the countries of the region and regional and subregional organizations in addressing governance and security challenges;
Peacebuilding and peace consolidation efforts by regional and subregional entities and other partners continue;

Political and technical-level engagements with UNOCA in support of the Gulf of Guinea Commission and the Interregional Coordination Centre for Maritime Safety and Security in the Gulf of Guinea continue;
Political commitment on the part of national, regional and international partners to work with the United Nations in the context of the United Nations integrated strategy for the Sahel;
Governments in the region remain willing to engage with UNOWAS and other partners to improve human rights and rule of law.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the table of deliverables reflects updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
Sustained dialogue and continuous regional engagements in West Africa and the Sahel

In 2025, in the aftermath of the withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger from ECOWAS, UNOWAS conducted sustained bilateral dialogue with the three countries and with ECOWAS. The mission’s efforts contributed to sustained engagement between the Alliance of the Sahel States (AES) countries and ECOWAS. One example of such engagement was the freezing of the restrictions on free movement of people, goods and services. Moreover, in support of the ECOWAS conflict prevention and peacebuilding mandate, and in line with the UNOWAS-ECOWAS Memorandum of Understanding, UNOWAS participated in ECOWAS-led missions and high-level consultations that contributed to supporting efforts to restore constitutional order in Guinea-Bissau following the coup d’état in November 2025 and easing institutional tensions in Liberia. UNOWAS also pursued engagement with the revitalized African Union Mission for Mali and the Sahel (MISAHEL) towards fostering regional dialogue.

Result 1: enhanced regional and subregional partnerships to respond to cross-border and cross-cutting security challenges – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, the mission’s good offices and advocacy efforts contributed to enhancing regional and subregional partnerships to respond to cross-border and cross-cutting security challenges. Despite the withdrawal of members of ECOWAS, regional and subregional partnerships showed capacity to sustain dialogue and collective responses contributing to a more predictable environment for security coordination and crisis management which helped to limit spillover, reduce misunderstanding between neighbouring States, and preserve space for civilian protection and humanitarian access.

In 2027, UNOWAS will continue working towards the establishment of an annual dialogue platform of West African Ministries of Foreign Affairs to enhance partnerships to respond to cross-border security challenges.

children.text: Result 2: conducive environment for peaceful and inclusive electoral processes in West Africa and the Sahel – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, the Special Representative sustained engagement with all key political stakeholders to advocate for peaceful and inclusive elections in Cote d'Ivoire. He undertook two missions during which he encouraged dialogue and confidence-building among political actors to strengthen trust in the electoral process and mitigate the risk of violence, which contributed to reinforcing collaboration channels between stakeholders.

In 2027, UNOWAS will conduct technical and high-level missions in countries where elections will take place, including in Nigeria and The Gambia, as well as in countries where key elections are scheduled to take place in 2028, including in Ghana and Sierra Leone.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the mission was that rebuilding trust among regional stakeholders requires sustained and multilayered engagement. In applying this lesson, the mission will continue to adopt a multilayered approach and work closely with ECOWAS, the AES, and their Member States to encourage continuous dialogue and broadening of communication channels.

2.	United Nations Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The United Nations Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia is responsible for supporting national authorities in identifying and addressing threats to regional peace and security. The open-ended mandate was defined through an exchange of letters between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council (S/2007/279 and S/2007/280). The mission plays a central role in preventive diplomacy in Central Asia and provides a platform for regional dialogue on the pressing challenges to security and stability.

The main function of the Regional Centre is to strengthen conflict prevention in Central Asia through liaison with the Governments and, with their concurrence, engaging with the parties concerned on promoting preventive diplomacy; providing capacity building in preventive diplomacy through various activities; monitoring and analysing the situation on the ground, providing the Secretary-General with updates relating to conflict prevention; maintaining contact with regional organizations, encouraging their peace-making efforts and facilitating coordination and information exchange, with due regard to their specific mandates; providing a political framework and leadership for preventive activities of the United Nations country teams and supporting efforts of the resident coordinators and representatives of the United Nations system in promoting an integrated approach to preventive diplomacy and humanitarian assistance; and maintaining close contact with the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan to ensure a comprehensive analysis of the situation in the wider region.
The Regional Centre’s current work is guided by a five-year programme of action for the period 2026–2030, which was developed in consultations with the Central Asian states.
Programme of work
Objective
The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to enhance regional security and stability in Central Asia.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

Carry out good offices functions for preventive diplomacy in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, as well as monitor and analyse regional developments in Central Asia and the wider geographical context, while maintaining contact with regional organizations and other entities of the United Nations system;
Organize an annual meeting of deputy ministers of foreign affairs of Central Asia and convene expert forums to advise the annual consultative meetings of the Central Asian Heads of State;
Advance political participation of women through the engagement of senior women political leaders in the Central Asia Women Leaders’ Caucus regional platform;

Promote arrangements on transboundary water management in the region, support initiatives and dialogue on water, energy and environmental and climate cooperation, and help to address challenges relating to transboundary water and climate change in line with the new strategy to support regional cooperation on water-energy, environment and climate for 2026-2030;

Implement the joint project with the Office of Counter-Terrorism based on the updated Joint Plan of Action for the Implementation of the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy in Central Asia;
Continue the efforts of the Regional Centre to engage young people through the Preventive Diplomacy Academy;

Support the Central Asian States in addressing emerging threats to security and stability and the other external risk factors, including by maintaining close contact with the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan to ensure comprehensive analysis of the situation in the region.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

Improved regional cooperation and capacity in addressing transnational threats of terrorism, violent extremism conducive to terrorism, drug trafficking and organized crime, as well as coping with regional challenges concerning the management of water resources and climate change;

Political will to sustain the progress of the Governments of the Central Asian States regarding deeper engagements in promoting peace and stability through enhanced cooperation and trust-building in the region, including on high-level platforms such as the consultative meeting of Heads of State.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission maintains cooperation with the Commonwealth of Independent States, the European Union, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, as well as  the International Fund for Saving the Aral Sea, among others. The Regional Centre continues exchanges with the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-building Measures in Asia and the Collective Security Treaty Organization on topics of common interest. It cooperates with relevant actors, including international financial institutions such as the World Bank. Such cooperation highly conducive to meaningful exchanges and coordination to avoid duplication and to look for synergy and complementarity.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, and to streamline the prevention efforts in the region, the Regional Centre cooperates closely with the resident coordinators in the five countries, the Development Coordination Office and other UN entities represented in the region, including UNOCT, UNDP, UN-Women, UNODC, CTED, UNESCO, UNECE and ESCAP. The mission regularly shares information and coordinates activities with the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
The continued commitment of the five Governments of the region to preventive diplomacy and strengthening regional dialogue and cooperation on issues of common concern;

The five countries of the region continue to monitor developments in Afghanistan and enhance preparedness to potential threats and risks of violent extremism and terrorism, drug trafficking and a potential humanitarian crisis. They continue to provide and advocate for humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan.

The Regional Centre integrates a gender perspective into operational and programmatic activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. It encourages the countries to ensure gender balance in their national delegations and include gender-related issues in the agendas of regional expert-level workshops on preventive diplomacy and confidence-building for the states’ officials.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy (UNDIS) and its action plan, the mission will work to ensure that the concerns and experiences of persons with disabilities are an integral part of the design, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of all policies and programmes, so that persons with disabilities benefit equally. The UNDIS will be implemented internally through greater workforce diversity and a more inclusive physical environment, and externally through programming and stakeholder engagement.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the programme to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
Evaluation activities
In 2027, the mission is planning a self-evaluation of activities related to transboundary water management, and climate in the region.
Programme performance in 2025
Constructive and strengthened relations among the Central Asian States

In 2025, the Treaty on State Border between the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan and agreements between the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan on “eternal friendship” and the joint border junction, marked major milestones in strengthening regional peace and cooperation. The mission continued its political engagement to support efforts aimed at ensuring the long-term sustainability of the border agreements, should the concerned countries request further assistance. The mission also contributed to strengthened relations between the five countries of the region through convening annual meetings of the Deputy Foreign Ministers of the Central Asian states where information exchange and discussions on regional challenges took place. The mission also provided a platform on issues of shared concerns, including on the impact of the situation in Afghanistan on the region as well as transboundary waters, impact of climate, and women’s and youth engagement.

3.	United Nations support for the Cameroon-Nigeria Mixed Commission
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Cameroon-Nigeria Mixed Commission is responsible for facilitating the implementation of the judgment of the International Court of Justice of 10 October 2002 on the Cameroon-Nigeria boundary and territorial dispute. Its mandate includes supporting the demarcation of the land boundary and the delineation of the maritime boundary; facilitating the withdrawal of troops and transfer of authority in identified areas along the boundary; addressing the situation of the border populations affected by the demarcation process; and making recommendations on confidence-building measures to support them.

The current mandate of the United Nations support team to the Cameroon-Nigeria Mixed Commission derives from the exchange of letters between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council (S/2017/78 and S/2017/79) and subsequent exchanges of letters, including, most recently, S/2025/864 and S/2025/865. The current mandate calls for the preparation of a transition plan for the progressive handover of the activities of the Mixed Commission to the Joint Bilateral Commission and other subregional structures.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to achieve an orderly and peaceful implementation of the judgment of 10 October 2002 of the International Court of Justice delineating the course of the land and maritime boundary between Cameroon and Nigeria.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:
Support the parties in constructing the remaining boundary pillars along the land boundary;
Produce the final maps of the land boundary;
Finalize a boundary statement at the conclusion of the final mapping;

Jointly operationalize recommendations from the assessments on confidence-building initiatives for local communities affected by the demarcation process, and handover responsibility to the UN country teams in Cameroon and Nigeria as well as to national authorities;
Enhance cross-border cooperation and good practices in international boundaries management by sharing lessons learned from the Mixed Commission;
Strengthen bilateral cross-border cooperation through institutional agreements and joint engagement with Nigerian and Cameroonian authorities, supported by the African Union Border Programme;
Develop and transfer operational guidelines, technical specifications, field assessment methodologies, pillar documentation, databases and maps to national counterparts;
Promote the establishment of a joint Cameroon-Nigeria border management committee to ensure continued cooperation
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Physical demarcation of the Cameroon-Nigeria land boundary through the construction of boundary pillars;
Delivery of finalized maps covering the entire land boundary;
Production of a boundary statement recording the field coordinates of the emplaced pillars;

Cross-border stability, enhanced socio-economic resilience, improved living conditions for affected communities, and ensured a smooth transition of confidence-building initiatives to national partners and UN country teams in Cameroon and Nigeria;
Consensus between Cameroon, Nigeria and key stakeholders on best practices with respect to border management.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission will work with the national authorities of Cameroon and Nigeria to finalize the demarcation process between the two countries. This includes holding meetings, producing final maps, constructing remaining boundary pillars and preparing a boundary statement.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission will continue to collaborate with the United Nations country teams in Cameroon and Nigeria to jointly operationalize the consolidated joint needs assessment, resulting in tangible projects to strengthen local trust among communities affected by the border demarcation, promote peace and support sustainable cross-border development. Such coordination will result in a streamlined and coherent framework that improves resource mobilization and donor confidence, supporting a more effective, comprehensive approach to peacebuilding, development and cooperation in the border areas. The Mixed Commission secretariat is hosted within UNOWAS premises in Dakar, which provides administrative and logistical support. The Head of UNOWAS serves as the Chair of the Mixed Commission.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

The two parties, Cameroon and Nigeria, will continue to adhere to the judgment of the International Court of Justice and the workplan adopted by the Mixed Commission, as well as establish a bilateral mechanism to sustain the gains;
Safety, security and climate conditions will permit field operations to continue unimpeded;
Extrabudgetary resources, including additional voluntary contributions, will continue to be made available for border demarcation, pillar construction and confidence-building initiatives.

The Mixed Commission integrates a gender perspective into its operations, deliverables and results, as appropriate. Examples include targeting women’s and youth groups in community development projects related to potable water, employment capacity-building and access to the electricity network.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 contains no significant change arising from the UN80 initiative and reflects efforts of the programme to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner.
Programme performance in 2025
Political commitment to continued dialogue to resolve remaining disagreement areas

In 2025, the mission continued its collaboration with the parties to resolve the three long-standing areas of disagreement. As a result, various meetings were held, including the Sub-Commission on Demarcation meetings in Dakar and Geneva, as well as the Project Steering Committee meeting in Geneva. These sessions resolved the three remaining areas of disagreement, resulting in an agreement on the full land boundary and laying the groundwork for completing the demarcation process. Key outcomes also included the adoption of the provisional boundary line and coordinates, and the terms of reference for a field assessment mission collectively known as the “Geneva Agreement, 2025.” The field assessment mission was conducted at the end of the reporting period, with its report scheduled for adoption by the Sub-Commission in January 2026.

4.	Office of the United Nations Special Coordinator for Lebanon
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mandate of the Office of the United Nations Special Coordinator for Lebanon stems from Security Council resolution 1701 (2006), as well as subsequent decisions of the Council, including those contained in S/2007/85 and S/2007/86, S/PRST/2015/7, S/PRST/2016/10 and S/PRST/2025/1. The Special Coordinator is the representative of the Secretary-General vis-à-vis all Government and national counterparts, as well as regional, multilateral, and diplomatic entities based in Lebanon, and provides political guidance and promotes coherence across the Organization’s activities. The Deputy Special Coordinator leads the United Nations country team and humanitarian country team in his capacity as Resident Coordinator/Humanitarian Coordinator and oversees United Nations humanitarian and development activities in Lebanon.

The Security Council, in its resolution 2790 (2025), decided to extend for a final time the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) until 31 December 2026 and requested the Secretary-General to explore, by 1 June 2026, options for the future of the implementation of resolution 1701 (2006) after the withdrawal of UNIFIL. The Council welcomed the Cessation of Hostilities arrangement of 26 November 2024 (see S/2024/870) and requested the parties to faithfully implement its provisions, with the support of the United Nations Special Coordinator for Lebanon and UNIFIL, in line with their mandates.

In the context of the Office’s mandate and pending further clarification on the options for the future of the implementation of resolution 1701 (2006), the core objectives of resolution 1701 (2006) to be advanced by UNSCOL will include restoration and consolidation of the cessation of hostilities including through confidence-building measures and dialogue to reach negotiated solutions, assertion of a State monopoly on arms, elaboration of a national security strategy and architecture, implementation of the arms embargo, and delineation of Lebanon’s international borders, both with Israel and the Syrian Arab Republic, as well as support for Lebanese State institutions, including to respond to the socioeconomic and humanitarian impacts of the conflict.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to prevent and mitigate conflict between Israel and Lebanon and work towards an eventual permanent ceasefire and to extend and consolidate State authority in support of the territorial integrity, sovereignty and political independence of Lebanon.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

Exercise its good offices between the parties to preserve and consolidate the restoration of a cessation of hostilities, prevent a relapse into conflict and advance the full implementation of resolution 1701 (2006);

Intensify efforts to resolve outstanding obligations of all parties under resolution 1701 (2006) to secure a permanent ceasefire and long-term solution to the conflict, including through the restoration of Lebanon’s territorial integrity and delineation of Lebanon’s international borders;

Advocate for Lebanon’s political leadership to ensure the effective functioning of State institutions to provide essential services for its citizens, preparations towards the conduct of transparent, inclusive and credible parliamentary elections, the adoption of a macroeconomic stabilization programme and implementation of a comprehensive reform and recovery programme;

Facilitate urgently required humanitarian, recovery and reconstruction imperatives necessitated by hostilities and mitigate the impact of continued volatility in the Syrian Arab Republic on the security, stability and refugee situation in Lebanon, including through, inter alia, support for bilateral cooperation initiatives;

Support the accelerated extension of State authority and assertion of a State monopoly on arms across Lebanese territory, intensify engagement with national political stakeholders and with international partners to facilitate the disarmament of non-State armed groups through a whole-of-government approach, and engagement with Syrian authorities on unresolved border, security and judicial issues, in order to strengthen the State security presence along border points and ensure the effective enforcement of the arms embargo.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
An enduring cessation of hostilities with the requisite political support in Lebanon and Israel;
Direct or indirect negotiations between Lebanon and Israel to address outstanding obligations under resolution 1701 (2006) towards an eventual permanent ceasefire;

Effective Lebanese State institutions in place and comprehensive structural reforms initiated to put the country on the path to recovery, uphold its democratic principles and strengthen good governance;

The State’s effective exercise of authority over all Lebanese territory, including through the strengthened deployment of the Lebanese Armed Forces, and steps taken to secure its borders and other entry points;
Lebanon’s implementation of a political framework that establishes a State monopoly over the possession, transfer and production of arms;
Engagement on the Lebanon-Israel and Lebanon-Syrian Arab Republic tracks to delineate the international borders of Lebanon in its entirety, including by addressing the issue of the Shab’a Farms.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission coordinates with the League of Arab States, the European Union and international financial institutions such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund to ensure coherence and alignment in political advocacy. The Special Coordinator engages international and regional stakeholders as part of her good offices mandate, to help build trust and defuse tensions, mobilize broad support for Lebanon’s stability and promote political and diplomatic processes towards the full implementation of resolution 1701 (2006).

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, pending a decision by the Security Council on the options for the future of the implementation of resolution 1701 (2006) after UNIFIL withdraws, UNSCOL will lead efforts in support of the implementation of resolution 1701 (2006) to maintain the cessation of hostilities and to strengthen the extension of State authority across all of Lebanon’s territory. Leveraging the presence of all UN entities, the mission brings all available political, security and development tools to bear in a coordinated and harmonized manner in support of Lebanon’s recovery, stability, and extension of its State authority. The mission also contributes to the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework and leads its peace and governance results group, including work on areas related to good governance, support to law enforcement and security entities, peacebuilding, and joint initiatives to enhance trust building and youth empowerment.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
International consensus on Lebanon will continue to be challenged;
Political divisions and deepened sectarian tensions may hinder effective government decision-making and undermine internal dialogue and economic and governance reforms;
The prolonged socioeconomic crisis, compounded by the impact of the conflict, and its humanitarian repercussions will remain a source of instability and social unrest;

Lebanon’s internal stability and security will remain vulnerable to the volatile regional situation, highlighting the need for bilateral engagement to address potential security concerns and shield the country from spillover;
Internal dynamics in the Syrian Arab Republic, as well as Lebanese-Syrian relations, are likely to dictate cross-border movements;

Relations between Lebanon and Israel will remain fraught, underlining the imperative for engagement of the parties in a political process to consolidate an enduring cessation of hostilities and address the underlying causes of the conflict within the framework of resolution 1701 (2006) towards pursuit of a permanent ceasefire;

Extension of State authority in Lebanon and along its borders will continue to be affected by political will, other law-and-order requirements and financial, political and logistical challenges faced by the State security institutions in asserting the State’s monopoly on arms.

In coordination with national stakeholders and UN entities, the mission integrates a gender perspective, as appropriate, and is working to promote the adoption of measures to protect and prevent violence against women and enhance women’s political leadership and representation through a range of initiatives, including legislative reforms (e.g. special temporary measures for elections) to promote women’s political participation, as well as women’s engagement in inclusive peace dialogue networks at the local and national levels. Together with relevant partners in the United Nations country team, the mission supports networks engaged in reconciliation, conflict prevention, inclusive community dialogue and mediation.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will promote and mainstream disability inclusion in the implementation of its mandate within its internal work practices and operations and in broader joint UN system engagements. The mission also implements a specific action plan for disability inclusion and through active involvement within the broader UN System Working Group for disability inclusion at both local and global levels.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative
The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
Evaluation activities

In 2025, UNSCOL together with UN Women, conducted a joint assessment study of women’s leadership and representation within Lebanese political parties. The results of the study served as a joint impact-driven evaluation of the UN advocacy efforts in support of women’s political participation. In addition, UNSCOL conducted an assessment of the overall UN support to Lebanese law enforcement and security institutions. This exercise was jointly conducted with UNIFIL, UNDP, UNOPS, IOM, UNHCR, UN Women, UNODC, and the RCO. In response to the evaluation of women representation, UNSCOL is strengthening its engagement with political parties and emerging pro-change political groups to advocate for enhanced women representation. In response to evaluation of support to law enforcement institutions, the mission is widening its outreach to all national security agencies and potential partners to better coordinate the UN support and avoid duplication.
Programme performance in 2025
Consolidation of the cessation of hostilities

In 2025, the Special Coordinator exercised her good offices with relevant stakeholders in Lebanon, Israel, the region and beyond, to promote confidence-building measures to consolidate the cessation of hostilities arrangement of November 2024 to promote enduring security and stability for communities on both sides of the Blue Line. Through public and closed-door channels, the Special Coordinator urged all parties to leverage the momentum provided by the cessation of hostilities arrangement to take concrete steps towards negotiated solutions to advance long-stalled provisions of Security Council resolution 1701 (2006), including through, inter alia, promoting and supporting the commencement of a civilian dialogue track.

The Special Coordinator also offered her good offices to support the Government of Lebanon in its effort to establish exclusive State control over weapons, including through mobilization of international support for the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) to ensure a strengthened presence and effective deployment south of the Litani River as a critical first step, while continuing work towards the full extension of State authority across all of Lebanon’s territory.

Result 1: political and diplomatic efforts to delineate Lebanon’s international borders – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, the mission supported political and diplomatic efforts and regularly engaged with the parties to address outstanding provisions of resolution 1701 (2006) and consolidate the 2024 cessation of hostilities arrangement towards creating the space for progress on longer-term objectives, such as the restoration of Lebanon’s territorial integrity, including through the withdrawal of the Israel Defense Forces from north of the Blue Line, and resolution of disputed border areas. The resolution of disputed border areas witnessed some renewed interest without meeting the planned target for 2025. Meanwhile, building on conducive openings with Syria, the mission supported the nascent exploration of border delineation initiatives between the two countries.

For 2027, the mission will employ its good offices to support the restoration and consolidation of a cessation of hostilities, including through leveraging the momentum for dialogue between the parties to reach negotiated solutions on outstanding provisions of resolution 1701 (2006), including the disarmament of non-State armed groups, the withdrawal of Israeli forces from north of the Blue Line, and a border dispute resolution as potentially significant aspects of a long-term solution. In parallel, the mission will leverage windows of opportunity, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders, to facilitate progress towards a border delineation track between Lebanon and Syria.

children.text: Result 2: extension and consolidation of State authority and strengthened governance to advance Lebanon’s stability and recovery – Proposed programme plan for 2027

For 2027, the mission will build on Lebanon’s Government decisions to achieve the nationwide state monopoly on arms. Noting potential gaps following the end of UNIFIL’s operations on 31 December 2026, UNSCOL will continue to lead UN efforts to mobilize international assistance to empower Lebanon’s security institutions and to advance progress towards a national security strategy and related architecture. In support of Lebanon’s overall stability and recovery, the mission will advocate for the effective and uninterrupted functioning of governance institutions and for tangible progress in the reform and macroeconomic stabilization track.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the mission was that consolidating the cessation of hostilities was not insulated from the volatile international and regional context, which impacted the calculations of all parties and ultimately led to the collapse of the cessation of hostilities arrangement. The mission will, therefore, continue to exercise its good offices with stakeholders in the region and beyond to shield progress from externalities. The growth of cross-cutting and interconnected challenges facing Lebanon, which span the humanitarian, development, political and security fields, have reinforced the need for the deeper integration between related pillars of the UN’s work, which UNSCOL will be prioritizing in its working methods, communication products, planning and assessments, among other streams of work.

5.	United Nations Regional Office for Central Africa
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

UNOCA is responsible for the prevention of conflicts and the consolidation of peace and security in Central Africa. The mandate derives from an exchange of letters between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council (S/2009/697 and S/2010/457). In another exchange of letters (S/2024/648 and S/2024/649), the mandate was extended until 31 August 2027.

The mandate for the period 2024–2027 encompasses four objectives, namely: (a) monitor political and security developments in Central Africa and carry out good offices on behalf of the Secretary-General in order to prevent and resolve conflicts, to help to sustain peace and to advise the Secretary-General and United Nations entities in the region on sustaining peace issues in Central Africa; (b) enhance subregional capacities for conflict prevention and mediation in countries of the subregion, with due attention given to the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, including human rights and gender dimensions; (c) support and enhance United Nations efforts in the subregion, as well as regional and subregional initiatives on peace and security, including from human rights and gender perspectives; and (d) enhance coherence and coordination in the work of the United Nations in the subregion on peace and security.
The mission serves as the secretariat of the United Nations Standing Advisory Committee on Security Questions in Central Africa.
Programme of work
Objective
The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to prevent conflict and consolidate peace and security in the Central Africa subregion.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

Engage in good offices activities to help countries to prevent political crises and election-related violence and peacefully resolve conflicts and crises stemming from political processes, including political transitions, and promote inclusive, peaceful and credible elections;

Leverage its partnership with subregional organizations, especially the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS) in conflict prevention, mediation and early warning, ensuring the participation of women, young people and other actors in inclusive peacebuilding and sustaining peace efforts, including the implementation of the regional strategy on hate speech, and addressing the adverse effects of climate change on peace and security;

Cooperate with the Lake Chad Basin Commission on the revision of the territorial action plans that will guide the implementation of the revised Regional Strategy for the Stabilization, Recovery and Resilience of the Boko Haram-Affected Areas of the Lake Chad Basin Region;

Address cross-regional peace and security challenges, including farmer-herder dynamics, the crisis in the Lake Chad Basin and maritime piracy in the Gulf of Guinea, in close coordination with United Nations entities in Central and West Africa;

Carry out regular early warning analysis to inform preventive diplomacy and good offices efforts for peace and security in Central Africa, and mobilize support for preventive diplomacy, in collaboration with ECCAS and United Nations entities;

Enhance the coherence of the work of the United Nations on peace and security issues in Central Africa through regular consultations with relevant United Nations entities in the subregion, coordinate the efforts of United Nations entities geared towards the implementation of the regional conflict prevention framework and in line with commitments of the Pact for the Future, and support the country teams in adopting and/or rolling out national sustaining peace strategies aligned with the framework;

Support the regular ministerial meetings of United Nations Standing Advisory Committee on Security Questions in Central Africa as a platform for confidence-building between Member States to discuss threats and challenges to regional peace and security, with a view to preventing or addressing conflicts, crises or inter-State tensions.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

Peaceful and credible electoral processes in the subregion, with relevant prevention mechanisms in place for potential election-related violence, Initiation or continuation of inclusive political dialogue processes, assisted by joint early-warning and good offices by the mission and ECCAS in countries holding elections or facing a political crisis;

The United Nations Standing Advisory Committee on Security Questions in Central Africa is contributing to reinforced cooperation and coordination among ECCAS member States, regional organizations and other key stakeholders of the subregion;

A shared understanding of key peace and security challenges and priorities among United Nations entities in Central Africa, integrating emerging drivers of conflicts, including the impact of climate change and environmental degradation;
Enhanced coordination of United Nations efforts in support of regional and subregional initiatives on peace and security and governance;

Improved interregional coordination of efforts between Central and West Africa on maritime security in the Gulf of Guinea, the impact of climate change on peace and security, farmer-herder dynamics and the crisis in the Lake Chad Basin region.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission carries out joint analyses and activities on cross-regional peace and security challenges with other regional and subregional organizations. Early warning analysis and good offices are carried out, to the extent possible, jointly or in consultation with ECCAS.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission works closely with the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Great Lakes Region, United Nations Office for West Africa and the Sahel (UNOWAS), the United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA), the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) and other relevant United Nations entities with respect to cross-border and transregional challenges to peace and security, in order to avoid duplication and ensure coherence and enhance synergies. Country-specific early warning and good offices activities are carried out in close coordination with the resident coordinators concerned.
With regard to external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

ECCAS institutional reform becomes increasingly more operational, with all peace and security institutions and mechanisms established and provided with adequate resources for their functioning in the context of new leadership of the sub-regional organization;

UNOCA and ECCAS maintain or strengthen their cooperation and regular consultations and adopt and roll out a joint plan of action, within the framework of a new memorandum of understanding between ECCAS and the United Nations on peace and security issues;

ECCAS member States remain committed to establishing a regional governance framework, work towards the adoption and implementation of regional governance standards and mechanisms and solicit or accept the support of UNOCA and regional and international partners;

The elections scheduled in the countries of the region, are held according to the constitutional and legal time frames and the countries concerned accept the political engagement of UNOCA and ECCAS to defuse tensions, prevent election-related violence and resolve election-related crises;

ECCAS and its member States show a commitment to the involvement of civil society actors, including the regional Coalition of Civil Society Organizations for Peace and Conflict Prevention in Central Africa, the Coalition of Youth, Peace and Security in Central Africa and women’s organizations, in the activities of ECCAS in the realm of peace and security, including early warning, conflict prevention and peacebuilding. The Coalition of Civil Society Organizations becomes fully operational, with adequate human resources, and is supported by ECCAS member States and partners;

ECCAS member States develop, adopt and begin the implementation of a conflict-sensitive regional strategy on climate change and resilient development and regional regulation on pastoralism and transhumance in Central Africa to address the impacts of climate change on peace and security, while strengthening national and local mechanisms to prevent and peacefully resolve farmer-herder conflicts and promote peaceful cross-border transhumance;

The international community increases support to Chad in light of the continued influx of Sudanese refugees and its impact on social cohesion and resources with a view to helping Chad responding to those challenges.

The mission works with other relevant United Nations entities and external partners to reinforce the capacities of women in decision-making and in mediation. It will continue to support the operationalization and build the capacity of the ECCAS network of women mediators established in December 2021 and endorsed by the Heads of State in January 2022. UNOCA will also support ECCAS in the finalization and dissemination of the updated Regional Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission advocates for political and electoral processes in the region to be disability-sensitive, by encouraging Member States to take appropriate measures to facilitate the participation of persons with disabilities. The mission also encourages and supports experience-sharing between the States of the region on disability inclusion, thus facilitating the adoption of measures that take into consideration the specificities of the regional and national contexts. The mission will also target partners such as organizations or associations of persons with disabilities as part of its capacity-building activities.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the table of deliverables reflects updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
Strengthened national capacities in reducing electoral and institutional tensions in Chad and Gabon

In 2025, through the good offices of the Special Representative of the Secretary‑General, UNOCA intensified diplomatic engagement across Central Africa to accompany political transitions and support electoral processes. In Chad, the Office engaged national authorities on post‑transition priorities, including decentralization, disarmament, demobilization and reintegration, stabilization and inclusive development, following the country’s completion of its political transition and the holding of legislative, provincial, municipal and senatorial elections between December 2024 and March 2025, which marked the full restoration of constitutional order.

In Gabon, UNOCA maintained regular dialogue with transitional authorities and political actors, underscoring the importance of institutional reforms and supporting preparations for legislative, senatorial and local elections, which represented key steps in consolidating progress made after the presidential election of April 2025 toward restoring constitutional governance. Across the subregion, UNOCA also advanced initiatives aimed at expanding the participation of women and young people, including technical support to a mentoring programme for women’s political leadership in Gabon and regional youth engagement on peace and security priorities.

Strengthened regional capacities for conflict prevention and mediation in Central Africa – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, UNOCA strengthened regional capacities for conflict prevention and mediation by supporting ECCAS‑led early warning and preventive diplomacy mechanisms and convening regional stakeholders through the United Nations Standing Advisory Committee on Security Questions in Central Africa. Targeted capacity‑building for civil society organizations, women and youth actors, and journalists enhanced coordination, inclusive engagement and collective responses to emerging political and security risks across the subregion.

In 2027, building on close cooperation with ECCAS, UNOCA will continue supporting subregional mechanisms that reinforce early warning, dialogue and coordinated responses to political and security challenges. Additionally, UNOCA will deepen cooperation with regional and international stakeholders on thematic priorities such as climate‑related security risks, transhumance‑related conflicts and cross‑border stabilization, informed by field assessments, engagement, local action, and joint workshops conducted in the subregion.
Lessons learned and planned change

A lesson for the mission was the importance of structured and sustained engagement with regional and subregional organizations, particularly during periods of institutional transition on the side of ECCAS, to preserve continuity and enhance the effectiveness of preventive diplomacy. The change in ECCAS leadership in 2025 underscored the need for proactive engagement to align priorities, leverage complementarities and strengthen joint ownership of peace and security initiatives. In applying this lesson, UNOCA will deepen its strategic partnership with the renewed ECCAS leadership and its member States, while reinforcing coordination with United Nations presences, country teams and relevant international, national and civil society stakeholders.
