6.	United Nations Support Mission in Libya
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

UNSMIL is an integrated special political mission established by the Security Council in resolution 2009 (2011). The Mission is mandated to support Libya’s transition and post-conflict efforts, including through the facilitation of an inclusive political process. The mandate of the Mission is defined in Security Council resolution 2542 (2020), and renewed by its subsequent resolutions, including most recently resolution 2796 (2025), by which the Council extended the mandate of the Mission until 31 October 2026.

In its resolution 2796 (2025), the Security Council encouraged UNSMIL to implement the recommendations of the 2025 Strategic Review (S/2025/611), including to: (a) place the support of a political solution to the Libyan conflict at the core of the Mission’s mandate and streamline its workstreams to that end; (b) establish a more consistent presence across Libya, including targeted expansions in Benghazi and Sabha, while maintaining a cost neutral realignment and within existing resources; (c) increase engagement in eastern and southern Libya with key stakeholders to support reunification efforts; (d) establish a dedicated economic unit within UNSMIL; (e) assume a leading role in international engagement on Libya, particularly in relation to the Berlin Process, encouraging its full participation and continued evolution and inclusivity to further advance the process; and recognize that UNSMIL’s engagement on human rights and the rule of law remains integral to the country’s political process.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this Mission contributes, is to support an inclusive Libyan-led political process and rights-based national reconciliation, conflict prevention and peacebuilding efforts; strengthen rule of law institutions, transitional justice processes and State-building efforts to optimize readiness for planning and implementing credible, transparent and inclusive elections; advance human rights, gender equality and women’s and youth political participation; support the reform of the security sector, disarmament, demobilization and reintegration efforts and the further implementation of the October 2020 ceasefire agreement.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Mission will:

Provide mediation and good offices in support of a Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process facilitated by the United Nations, in line with the political roadmap and its three core pillars announced by the Special Representative in August 2025;

Address long-term drivers of conflict, and work towards government unification and strengthen inclusive political engagement with diverse stakeholders, including women, youth, and persons with disabilities, in Libya taking into consideration the recommendations of the Structured Dialogue of 2025-2026;
Provide technical assistance to the High National Elections Commission in conducting transparent and inclusive national and municipal elections;

Support inclusive, victim-centred and rights-based national reconciliation processes based on transitional justice principles, capacity-building for reconciliation bodies and the facilitation of dialogue among diverse Libyan actors, including civil society, women, persons with disabilities and youth;

Establish a more consistent presence across Libya, including targeted expansions in Benghazi and Sabha within a cost-neutral realignment and existing resources, while increasing engagement with key stakeholders in eastern and southern Libya;
Strengthen the rule of law and accountability by supporting Libya’s judiciary and prosecutorial systems, including their critical role in ensuring justice for all Libyans;

Promote and protect human rights by monitoring, reporting and addressing violations, with a focus on sexual violence in conflict and violations against vulnerable groups, and by ensuring civic space for political participation;

Advance security sector reform, by supporting Libyan-led and Libyan owned initiatives that reduce the risk of a return to widespread conflict, including through confidence-building measures, dialogue among security and military actors, and engagement with legislative bodies on national security legislation, with a view to the reunification of security and military institutions under civilian oversight;

Facilitate disarmament, demobilization and reintegration through support to national coordination mechanisms and civil society engagement, including technical assistance for planning and capacity development in mine action coordination and weapons and ammunition management;

Support the 5+5 Joint Military Commission and its subcommittees, by facilitating confidence-building measures, dialogue, and reconciliation among armed actors to prevent violence and conflict escalation and support the implementation of the ceasefire agreement, including progress on the withdrawal of foreign forces, foreign fighters, and mercenaries, through engagement at national and local levels;

Support progress towards a unified national budget and unified institutions which promote independent and transparent economic and oversight institutions, in close cooperation with the international community, UN country team and international financial institutions;

Facilitate inclusive dialogue on economic governance and political economy dynamics to support a shared national economic vision and advance reforms that address conflict drivers and deliver tangible benefits for all Libyans, including women, youth, and persons with disabilities;

Engage with neighbouring countries, including Sahel countries, in support of regional cooperation and stabilization efforts, and ensuring their perspectives and security concerns are reflected in efforts to advance the Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

An inclusive Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process leading to elected, unified, functional and representative state institutions, including economic institutions, contributing to political stability, sound economic governance, and the protection of civic space as an enabler of credible elections and legitimate institutions;
Enhanced accountability of institutions, promotion of the rule of law throughout the country, and reconciliation and transitional justice processes promoting and protecting human right;

Progress toward unified security and military institutions operating under civilian oversight, including improved coordination and accountability among security actors and professional defence and security forces, through support to the implementation of the ceasefire agreement and initiatives that reduce the risk of a return to widespread conflict, in support of the political process and electoral stability.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the Mission cooperates with relevant local, national, regional and international partners and regional organizations, including the African Union, the League of Arab States and the European Union in support of the Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Mission and the United Nations country team will continue to implement the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, extended by one additional year. Coordination modalities will be adjusted as necessary to ensure coherence between political engagement and development priorities, taking into account the evolving context and system-wide guidance.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

The Libyan Political Agreement of December 2015, Security Council resolutions 2510 (2020) and 2796 (2025), the conclusions of the Berlin Conference on Libya, the October 2020 Ceasefire Agreement, the Libyan Political Dialogue Forum Tunis roadmap and accompanying outputs and the UNSMIL political roadmap announced in 2025 will remain the guiding framework for United Nations support in Libya, including efforts to enable an inclusive political process and the conditions for elections;

Economic governance challenges, including limited oversight, weak transparency and accountability, and constrained institutional capacity, are expected to persist. External factors include oil price fluctuations affecting revenues and regional dynamics;

Progress in implementing the October 2020 Ceasefire Agreement, including the withdrawal of foreign forces, foreign fighters and mercenaries, is expected to remain uneven and dependent on sustained commitment by Libyan and external actors. The truce agreed between armed groups in western Libya following the May 2025 clashes in Tripoli will continue to hold;

UNSMIL’s efforts will be shaped by the willingness of Libyan actors to engage in confidence-building measures, dialogue, and steps toward unification and reform of security institutions under civilian oversight, as well as broader regional dynamics;

The human rights situation in Libya will remain challenging, particularly in strengthening the rule of law, ensuring accountability for violations, and protecting civic space. The marginalization of women in political and reconciliation processes will continue to constrain peacebuilding;

Institutional weaknesses and divisions among the country’s security actors are expected to persist, continuing to create security vacuums and ungoverned spaces that may be exploited by violent extremist organizations, thereby increasing the risk of terrorist activity;

The security situation is expected to remain fragile due to the proliferation of weapons and armed actors, the absence of unified security/military institutions, and competition among armed groups, compounded by smuggling and trafficking networks;

The humanitarian situation is expected to evolve unevenly, shaped by security and political developments. While internal displacement may remain limited, vulnerabilities among internally displaced persons and returnees will persist in areas with weak services and insecurity. Continued conflict in Sudan is likely to sustain or increase protection pressures related to the influx of Sudanese refugees, alongside ongoing risks to migrants, refugees and asylum-seekers, including abuse, exploitation and limited access to protection and services;

Strategic partnerships will continue among the international community, including regional organizations and the United Nations, and are expected to continue in support of an inclusive Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process, while the United Nations sanctions regime continues to be applied.

The Mission integrates a gender perspective across operations. The revised 2026 Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security will guide efforts to strengthen gender integration and promote the full, equal and meaningful participation of women in political, electoral, governance and security processes. The Mission, together with the United Nations country team, will support women’s rights through advocacy, technical assistance and the promotion of gender-responsive legislation and policies, including measures addressing violence against women and service gaps affecting displaced, migrant and refugee women and girls.

The Mission will mainstream disability inclusion, promoting the full and meaningful participation of persons with disabilities in political dialogue, elections and public decision-making, including through targeted advocacy to address barriers to accessibility and participation.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the table of deliverables reflects updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Evaluation activities

The programme plan is informed by the recommendations of the recommendations of the Office of Internal Oversight Services evaluation of UNSMIL conducted in 2025. The proposed adjustments to objectives, strategies and deliverables reflect the recommendations of both reviews, with a focus on prioritization, alignment of mandate and resources, and more targeted political engagement.

In 2027, subject to available resources and capacities, UNSMIL will conduct an internal evaluation of the integration of women, peace and security and youth, peace and security agendas, and disability inclusion strategy within the political process, in line with relevant OIOS recommendations.
Programme performance in 2025
Strengthened rule of law institutions and transitional justice process protecting the rights of all people in Libya

In 2025, UNSMIL supported concrete steps to strengthen rule of law institutions and advance transitional justice through national‑level accountability engagement, reviews of the legal framework and capacity‑building for justice and security actors. As a result, national and local authorities, judicial institutions and representatives of victims convened to accelerate execution of national and international arrest warrants linked to the Tarhuna mass graves, enhance cooperation on extradition requests and support the resumption of excavations to identify missing persons. Stakeholders from Murzuq also convened in 2025 to address enforced disappearances and gross violations committed between 2019 and 2023. In addition, a joint committee, consisting of Libyan authorities, UNSMIL, UN agencies and other local technical parties, reviewed a preliminary draft law on missing persons to strengthen the legal basis for investigations, documentation and redress.

The Mission also organized specialised sessions for judges, prosecutors, investigators, prison staff and security actors covered international human rights and humanitarian law, international detention standards and related international processes. In addition, civil society reporting capacity was strengthened through structured engagement with international human rights mechanisms. This included the facilitation of civil society engagement with the Universal Periodic Review mechanism of the United Nations Human Rights Council, including through thematic civil society submissions. These actions improved the evidence base, legal readiness and institutional coordination needed for future accountability and victim-centred transitional justice pathways.

children.text: Result 2: a comprehensive road map for holding national elections, towards the establishment of unified, elected, legitimate, inclusive and functional government institutions contributing to political stability and reconciliation – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, UNSMIL delivered facilitation and good offices with key Libyan stakeholders to advance consensus on pathways toward elections and institutional unity. It established an Advisory Committee of Libyan experts to provide options to overcome electoral obstacles which later informed the launch of the Structured Dialogue (SD) in December 2025, aimed at addressing impediments to elections and underlying conflict drivers. In parallel, UNSMIL engaged political actors, including the House of Representatives and the High Council of State on reconstituting the High National Elections Commission (HNEC) and finalizing the electoral legal framework.

In 2027, UNSMIL will pursue an integrated political approach to advance a viable electoral roadmap and institutional unity. It will consolidate SD outcomes to support consensus on the electoral political framework and continue good offices to bridge divisions and enable a unified government through elections. UNSMIL will continue to engage all parties on human rights and rule of law issues as an integral part of the Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process. It will prioritize addressing arbitrary arrest and detention, the protection of civic space and civil society engagement as key enablers of the political and electoral processes.

children.text: Result 3: economic governance and political economy drivers of conflict are addressed in support of the political process – Proposed programme plan for 2027

In 2027, UNSMIL will advance the economic track as a core pillar of the political process integrating political economy analysis into mediation, negotiations and good offices to ensure that economic considerations directly inform engagement with political and security actors. It aims to realign incentives in support of institutional unity, reduce obstruction to reforms and create conditions conducive to credible national elections.
Lessons learned and planned change

A key lesson is that impact depends on tighter integration of economic incentive analysis across political, security and economic tracks. Stand-alone or purely economic initiatives had limited effect when not linked to political incentives, security arrangements or coordinated international engagement. In applying the lesson, UNSMIL will adopt a more integrated and targeted approach, prioritize reducing economic drivers of conflict by working with sovereign state institutions to curb rent-seeking incentives, addressing sources of patronage, and promoting transparent and accountable and rules-based economic decision-making consistent with human rights principles.

children.text: The proposed resource requirements for 2027 for UNSMIL amount to $83,067,400 (net of staff assessment) and would provide for the deployment of 167 out of the 234 authorized United Nations Guard Unit personnel ($5,109,000), salaries and related costs ($48,557,700) for the deployment of 220 international posts and positions (1 Under-Secretary-General, 2 Assistant Secretary-General, 7 D-1, 12 P-5, 42 P-4, 29 P-3, 2 P-2 and 125 Field Service) and 121 national posts and positions (27 National Professional Officer, 1 General Service (Other level) and 93 Local level), 5 international United Nations Volunteers and 7 government-provided personnel, inclusive of the establishment of 10 new posts and the proposed conversion of one post; and operational costs ($29,400,700).
Staffing requirements
For 2027, the proposed staffing complement reflects a net increase of 10 posts and positions.

In its resolution 2796 (2025), the Security Council encouraged the Mission to implement the recommendations of the Strategic Review (S/2025/611),  including, inter alia, the establishment of a more consistent presence across Libya through targeted expansions in Benghazi and Sabha, while maintaining a cost‑neutral realignment within existing resources, as well as the establishment of a dedicated economic section within UNSMIL. The Council further requested UNSMIL, in implementing the recommendations of the Strategic Review, to explore all avenues to enhance efficiency and redeploy existing resources, including, as appropriate, through the prioritization and reconfiguration of tasks and resources.

In this context, UNSMIL’s operational posture has been reassessed to ensure that leadership presence and staffing arrangements remain aligned with mandate delivery, prevailing security conditions and the evolving political context. The Libyan political process, reinvigorated through the political roadmap, requires a sustained presence across all regions of Libya. UNSMIL will operationalize this requirement through three mutually reinforcing directions:

Refocusing workstreams around the political process, with emphasis on security arrangements, economic governance, human rights and reconciliation, including the establishment of a dedicated economic unit within UNSMIL to work closely with the United Nations country team, including through the Results Group on Sustainable Economic Development;
Expanding field presence in eastern and southern Libya, specifically in Benghazi and Sabha, to ensure consistent engagement with national and local counterparts; and

Strengthening UNSMIL’s convening role to coordinate international support for the Libyan peace process. Cost‑efficiency measures have been pursued through adjustments to the Mission’s security posture, while continuing to ensure the safety and security of personnel. These measures included a review of the footprint of the United Nations Guard Unit and close protection requirements in light of the current operational and security context. Savings generated through reductions in troop levels were redeployed to support the Mission’s expanded presence in Benghazi and Sabha. In addition, efficiencies generated through the optimization of shared premises in Tunis and Libya, including office and accommodation space, have contributed to funding the expanded footprint in eastern and southern Libya, in line with the recommendations of the Strategic Review. UNSMIL has recalibrated its resource posture to preserve essential capacities and ensure the continuity of critical political, human rights and ceasefire‑related functions.
Expansion to Benghazi

The expansion to Benghazi will be accommodated through the establishment one post (National professional Officer), the conversion of one P-3 post to National professional Officer, the redeployment of 8 posts (2 P-4, 1 P-3, 2 Field Service, and 3 Local level), and the reassignment of one post (P-5), as follows:
(a) Establishment: it is proposed to establish one post of Assistant Public Information Officer (National Professional Officer) in the Public Information and Communications Section;
(b) Conversion: it is proposed to convert one post of Security Sector Reform Officer (P-3) to Associate Security Sector Reform Officer (National Professional Officer);
(c) Redeployment: it is proposed to redeploy the following posts from Tripoli to Benghazi:
one post of Political Affairs Officer (P-4) from the Political Affairs Service;
one post of Corrections Officer (P-4) and one post of Human Rights Officer (P-3) from the Human Rights and Rule of Law Service;
one Field Language Assistant (Local Level) from the former Ceasefire Monitoring Component;
two Close Protection Officers (Field Service) as Security Officers; and
two Field Security Assistants (Local Level);

(d) Reassignment: it is proposed to reassign one post of Senior Security Sector Reform Officer (P-5) from the former Ceasefire Monitoring Component to serve as Head of Office, Political Affairs (P-5), Benghazi Field Office, under the Office of the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General (Political).
Expansion to Sabha

The expansion of the Sabha field office will be accommodated through the establishment of seven posts (1 Field Service, 4 National Professional Officers and 2 Local Level) and the redeployment of 12 posts (1 P-4, 1 P-3, 5 Field Service and 5 Local level), as follows:
(a) Establishment: it is proposed to establish the following posts:
one Assistant Public Information Officer (National Professional Officer);
one Associate Human Rights Officer (National Professional Officer);
one Associate Security Sector Reform Officer (National Professional Officer);
one Facilities Management Assistant (Field Service);
one Medical Officer (National Professional Officer);
one Supply Assistant (Local Level); and
one Information Technology Assistant (Local Level);
(b) Redeployment: it is proposed to redeploy the following posts from Tripoli to Sabha:
one Electoral Officer (P-3);
one Military Liaison Officer (P-4);
one Close Protection Coordination Officer (Field Service) as Security Officer;
four Close Protection Officers (Field Service) as Security Officers;
Two Field Security Assistants (Local Level);
Three Security Radio Operators (Local level); and
Establishment of Ceasefire and Security Institutions Service

It is also proposed to establish a Ceasefire and Security Institutions Service as part of implementation of the Strategic Review recommendations. The revised structure reflects the merger of the former Ceasefire Monitoring Component and the Security Institutions Service, resulting in the consolidation of ceasefire‑related functions alongside existing mandates on security sector reform and disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration mandates. The proposal entails the redeployment of staff from the former Security Institutions Service (1 D-1, 1 P-5, 3 P-4, 2 P-3, 
1 Field Service and 1 National Professional Officer) and the Ceasefire Monitoring Component (2 P-4 and 2 P-3, inclusive of the 1 Military Liaison Officer (P-4) as mentioned in para 182 (b) above). This consolidation is intended to enhance regional outreach, strengthen engagement with military and security actors and improve the integration of policy development with field-level implementation, while ensuring organizational efficiency and avoiding duplication.
Establishment of an Economic Unit

In response to the recommendation of the Strategic Review to enhance United Nations engagement on economic governance, institutional integrity, and oversight – through establishing and operationalizing an Economic Section, the Mission proposes to establish the Economic Unit reporting to the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General/Resident Coordinator. The Unit would be staffed through the establishment of: (a) one post of Senior Economic Affairs Officer (P-5), providing senior-level policy engagement and strategic direction; and
(b) one post of Economic Affairs Officer (National Professional Officer), responsible for sustained liaison with Libyan institutions, contextual analysis and operational continuity.
Other proposed actions to improve coordination – Reassignment
Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General

It is proposed to reassign the Chief of Service, Ceasefire Monitoring Component (D-1) to the Principal Coordination Officer (D-1) in the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General to  provide senior-level coordination support to the SRSG, with a particular focus on integration of political and security-related files, internal coherence across Mission components, and serve as the technical lead of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for political/security engagement with senior national and international leadership. The incumbent would therefore act as a strategic bridge between the SRSG’s political good offices and the Mission’s security-related workstreams, helping to ensure that Mission efforts are sequenced, mutually reinforcing, and responsive to emerging risks.
Mission Support Service
Reassignment of the Associate Aviation Safety Officer (National Professional Officer) to Associate Data Analyst (National Professional Officer) in Tripoli

It is proposed to reassign the Associate Aviation Safety Officer (National Professional Officer) to the Associate Data Analyst (National Professional Officer) in Tripoli to support Mission’s operational activities through the management, and analysis of data to inform evidence‑based planning and decision‑making processes. The tasks of the Associate Data Analyst (National Professional Officer) will include the verification and management of operational data within the Mission’s operational activities, development of analytical products such as dashboards and mapping, provision of statistical trend analysis in support of in support of mandate implementation and data‑driven decision‑making processes and operational coordination.
Redeployment
Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General

It is proposed to redeploy one Legal Officer (P-4) from the Office of the Chief of Staff to perform a critical role advising the Head of Mission on all legal aspects of the Mission’s operations and its mandate. the Legal Officer would provide authoritative legal and policy advice on a diverse range of highly complex and novel substantive and procedural questions of law, which specifically include those related to administration and management, political and legal risks concerning the Mission’s mandated activities and other operational matters, and on legal-related policy matters in the context of the role of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General as Head of Mission and Designated Official for Libya.

It is proposed to redeploy one Field Language Assistant (Local level) from the Ceasefire Monitoring Component in Tripoli to provide invaluable support for reviewing and assessing communication that is received in Arabic, undertaking administrative duties with Libyan and international stakeholders that engage with the Office in Arabic, and provide administrative and other support senior staff, who will be engaging with Libyan interlocutors on a daily basis.
Office of the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Political

It is proposed to redeploy one Administrative Assistant (Field Service) from the Ceasefire Monitoring Component in Tunis to provide administrative, logistical, and coordination support to the Office of the DSRSG (Political), including support to meetings, reporting processes, and inter-component coordination. This adjustment enhances operational efficiency, strengthens support to senior leadership functions, and improves coordination across political processes while maintaining essential administrative capacity in support of the Mission’s mandate.
Office of the Chief of Staff

It is proposed to redeploy of one Field Language Assistant (Local Level) from the Ceasefire Monitoring Component in Tripoli, to the Office of Chief of Staff to support the administrative and coordination work of the Office with Arabic language tasks. support with interpretation and translation needs and with administrative arrangements for provision of language assistance. The incumbent will also provide direct interpretation support to the Chief of Staff in the engagements with national, local and de-facto authorities in regard to the expansion of the Mission’s presence in the east and south of Libya that was recommended by the Strategic Review and mandated by the Security Council.
Continuation of general temporary assistance positions
Office of the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Political

The UNSMIL Mine Action Unit supports the delivery of the Mission’s mine action mandate in line with Security Council resolution 2755 (2024) by providing technical expertise and support to the Libyan security institutions and the ceasefire mechanisms on mine action and weapons and ammunition management, and representing the Mission in relationship with relevant national mine action stakeholders and the United Nations country team. The temporary assistance position of Chief of Section, Programme Management (P-5), was established on 1 January 2022 in response to a recommendation from the Board of Auditors to improve the Secretariat leadership of UNSMIL mine action programme. Seven other temporary assistance positions were established under the UNSMIL mine action programme as of 1 January 2025 as part of the transition of mine action delivery from implementation in partnership with UNOPS to direct Secretariat delivery. These positions include two Programme Management Officers (P-4), one Programme Management Officer (P-3), one Associate Programme Management Officer (National Professional Officer), one Associate Administrative Officer (National Professional Officer), and one Data Analysis Officer (National Professional Officer). Given the continuity of the UNSMIL mine action programme in 2027, it is proposed that the seven temporary positions be continued to advance the UNSMIL mine action objectives as highlighted in the results of the Strategic Review in the most effective, cost-efficient and transparent manner.

The increase in requirements for 2027 compared with the appropriation for 2026 is attributable primarily to increased requirements for civilian personnel costs  resulting from : (a) the application of the latest salary rates for international staff, National Professional Officers and Local level staff; (b) the application of lower vacancy rates of 9.1 cent for international staff and 7.6 per cent for national General Service staff, compared  with the vacancy rates of 22.9 per cent and 26.1 per cent, respectively, applied in 2026; and (c) the proposed establishment of 10 posts (1 P-5, 1 FS, 6 National Professional Officers and 2 Local level). The increase is offset in part by: (a) application of a higher vacancy rate of 17.1 for National Professional Officers compared with 15.0 per cent budgeted in 2026: and (b) reduced requirements under operational costs and military contingents.
Under operational costs, a net decrease in requirements of $4,014,900 is attributable primarily to the following changes:

Facilities and infrastructure: the decrease in requirements of $3,943,600 is attributable primarily to reduced rental and maintenance costs for the Mission’s premises in Tripoli following renegotiation of terms in the renewal of the contract in 2025, as well as the cancellation of the construction of overhead protection after an additional assessment of the  security environment by the Department of Safety and Security. The decrease is offset in part by the requirements for the acquisition of critical generators, engineering and electrical equipment, as well as related spare parts and field defence supplies.

Air Operations: the decrease in requirements of $285,900 is attributable primarily to the reduction in the flight hours from 500 approved for 2026, to 411 proposed for 2027, based on analysis of the utilization of the fixed-wing aircraft over the preceding three financial periods. 7.	United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia is mandated to verify three key aspects of the Final Agreement for Ending the Conflict and Building a Stable and Lasting Peace, adopted in 2016 by the Government of Colombia and the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia – People’s Army (FARC-EP), comprising: (a) the reintegration of FARC-EP members into political, economic and social life (sect. 3.2 of the Agreement); (b) the implementation of personal and collective security and protection measures for ex-combatants, and comprehensive security and protection programmes for the communities and organizations in the territories (sect. 3.4 of the Agreement), and (c) the verification of the comprehensive rural reform (sect. 1 of the Agreement).

The Mission’s mandate is defined in Security Council resolutions 2366 (2017) and 2673 (2023). By its resolution 2798 (2025), the Security Council decided to extend the mandate until 31 October 2026. The Council further decided to discontinue the expansion of the mandate of the Verification Mission in Colombia to monitor ceasefires as set out in resolution 2694 (2023) and its associated resources. The Council requested the Secretary-General to ensure coordination and efficiencies, including by ensuring that other activities in country are carried out by the most appropriate UN system entity.

Pursuant to resolution 2798 (2025), the Secretary-General, in his report dated 26 December 2025 (S/2025/849), informed that as at 31 October 2025, the Mission had discontinued its verification activities pertaining to the ethnic chapter and the restorative sentences issued by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, as well as the expired ceasefire between the Government of Colombia and the Ejército de Liberación Nacional (ELN).
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Mission contributes, is to advance the effective implementation of the provisions of the Final Agreement concerning reintegration, security guarantees and comprehensive rural reform.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Mission will:

Apply a proactive and inclusive approach to verification, which includes advocacy, good offices and close engagement with the parties to the Final Agreement and relevant institutions and authorities at the international, national, regional and local levels, as well as vulnerable communities, with special attention to women, and children;

Conduct independent verification of the implementation of the Final Agreement and participate, jointly with the parties, in key forums and institutions created for the implementation of the Final Agreement;

Promote constructive dialogue and trust-building between the Government and the representatives of the former FARC-EP as the other signatory party of the Agreement  to address pending issues relating to peace implementation, foster collaborative communication with key interlocutors, including actors across the political spectrum, civil society and communities at risk (such as women, indigenous and Afro-Colombian peoples, and victims organizations), the private sector and the international community, to support the implementation of the Final Agreement;
Support the effective implementation of the Women, Peace and Security agenda at national and territorial levels to advance sustainable peace;
Provide good offices to support the implementation of the Final Agreement, monitor evolving conflict dynamics at local level between armed groups, and help to build and sustain peace in Colombia.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

Increased trust between the parties to the Final Agreement; sustainability of the reintegration process; opportunities for political participation; strengthened accountability and national efforts to foster security guarantees for former combatants, social leaders and communities; enhanced safe and productive land access and progress in the implementation of development plans with a territorial focus, with the active participation of local communities, for advances in the implementation of the comprehensive rural reform;

Enhanced State capacity, presence and responsiveness to promote collective and territorial protection approaches and better prevent and investigate attacks against former combatants, social leaders and communities; increased trust between the parties through tripartite coordination mechanisms at the national and local levels, while accounting for specific needs of communities at risk;

Enhanced coordination between government institutions, communities in situations of vulnerability, and women-led organizations; increased engagement of the international community, including the United Nations system;

Increased trust in the peace consolidation efforts, and progress in the comprehensive implementation of the Final Agreement to advance reconciliation, non-repetition and sustainable peace, contributing to a reduction in violence and improvements in the humanitarian situation in conflict-affected regions.

With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Mission engages extensively, building on synergies with other entities to support mandate implementation and peace consolidation in Colombia. Extensive engagement with the diplomatic community and regional organizations help to identify areas of mutual interest. At the national and local levels, the Mission strengthens ties with political, civil society and private sector actors, including community, religious, youth, women, peasant leaders, victims and persons with disabilities’ organizations. The Mission continues to bolster its relationships with Colombian departmental and local authorities, as they gain more responsibilities regarding the reintegration process, ensuring security guarantees for communities and supporting society’s participation in peace building.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Mission strengthened its coordination with the United Nations country team and the Resident Coordinator. The Mission also remains a member of the Strategic Committee of the United Nations Multi-Partner Trust Fund for Peace, thereby contributing to coherence across the peace and security and development pillars.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

Continued international support for the close engagement of the Mission and the United Nations system in the peace process, and continued commitment by national and local authorities and relevant parties remain to collaborating with the Mission;
The new governmental and legislative configuration emerging from the 2026 general elections will significantly influence the Mission’s work and the implementation of the Final Agreement;

National and local authorities remain engaged in increasing effective State presence; authorities, State entities and coordination mechanisms tasked with preventing and investigating security incidents remain committed to the prioritized populations in the Final Agreement;

Continued trust in the peace process and the comprehensive implementation of the Final Agreement, enabling advancements towards reconciliation and non-repetition, including for vulnerable communities, women, and children;
Continued efforts to advance the comprehensive rural reform with appropriate resource allocation and increased interinstitutional coordination.

The Mission integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, and ensures effective implementation of its gender parity directives and strategy. It also applies gender and intersectional analysis in verifying its core mandate, supporting effective referral pathways to responsible institutions for cases of gender-based and conflict-related sexual violence and - for the latter - contributing to improved reporting. The Mission provides support to the national action plan on Security Council resolution 1325 (2000) adopted in 2024, which is expected to strengthen the implementation of the gender provisions of the Final Agreement and reinforce the full, equal and meaningful participation of women in peacebuilding.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
Sustained national and community commitment to the implementation of the Final Agreement as the path to lasting peace

In 2025, Colombian institutions, former combatants, communities as well as international partners reaffirmed their commitment to the Final Agreement, as the country’s roadmap to lasting peace. The Mission operated under tight financial constraints, closing nine local offices amid renewed violent clashes, politically motivated violence, and uneven progress in peace dialogues, all of which significantly impacted the environment conducive to the implementation of the Final Agreement. In this context, the Mission’s monitoring and verification of the Final Agreement remained instrumental in sustaining peace dividends and confidence in the process. Through technical advice, advocacy, engagement and good office efforts, the Mission supported key peacebuilding achievements in advancing processes for economic reintegration, land acquisition, contributing to preventing former combatants’ return to violence.

Prior to the mandate renewal in October 2025, the Mission continued its engagement with relevant entities, including through its participation in the Monitoring and Verification Mechanism (MVM) and by enhancing information-sharing mechanisms across the transitional justice system. These efforts contributed to the operationalization of the MVM and helped reinforce coordination among institutions responsible for implementing transitional justice measures.
The mandate pertaining to the monitoring of restorative sentences has been discontinued, after which all related verification activities have ceased.

Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the Mission was that consistent and reliable land-related data would significantly enhance its ability to verify implementation of the comprehensive rural reform. Realignment of the proposed Verification Division

Following a comprehensive assessment conducted under the UN80 initiative and in line with Security Council resolution 2798 (2025), the Mission proposes a streamlined organizational structure aimed at enhancing efficiency, coherence, and effective delivery of its mandate. The proposed structure is organized around the Mission’s three core mandated areas: reintegration, rural reform, and security guarantees.

To strengthen strategic oversight, coordination and consistency across these areas, it is proposed to establish a Verification Division, reporting to the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, to provide integrated direction and guidance through three functionally distinct Sections: (a) the Verification of Reintegration Section; (b) the Verification of Rural Reform Section; and (c) the Verification of Security Guarantees Section. The Verification Division will also oversee the Regional Offices, Sub-offices, and Local Sites.

This realignment clarifies functional accountability, strengthens coordination across mandate pillars and supports a more streamlined and efficient management framework through the rationalization of senior-level functions.

Within this framework, the existing Verification of Reintegration and Rural Reform Office will be realigned to establish two distinct Sections: (a) a Verification of Reintegration Section, staffed through six existing posts (1 P-5, 1 P-4, 1 P-3 and 3 National Professional Officer) and (b) a Verification of Rural Reform Section, staffed through five existing posts (1 P-5, 1 P-4, 1 P-3 and 2 National Professional Officer). This realignment, through the redeployment of existing posts, responds to the increased scope, technical complexity and differentiated operational demands of the rural reform mandate and enables enhanced thematic focus, specialization, and accountability.

The Verification of Security Guarantees Office will be redesignated as the Verification of Security Guarantees Section to ensure consistency of organizational structure and nomenclature across the Mission. The Section will continue to be staffed through five existing posts (1 P-5, 1 P-4, 1 P-3 and 2 National Professional Officer), thereby maintaining operational continuity while supporting coherence within the Verification Division.

The proposed Verification Division will be staffed entirely through internal realignment and the redeployment of existing posts, based on the efficient use of resources and the preservation of institutional expertise. This approach ensures continuity of operations while improving functional alignment and effectiveness. Accordingly, the following posts actions are proposed:
Abolishment: it is proposed to abolish one post of D-1 Chief of the Security Guarantees Office, as part of the streamlining of senior leadership positions.

Redeployment: it is proposed to redeploy: (i)  six posts (1 P-5, 1 P-4, 1 P-3 and 3 National Professional Officer) from the former Verification of Reintegration and Rural Reform Office to the Verification of Reintegration Section; (ii) five posts (1 P-5, 1 P-4, 1 P-3 and 2 National Professional Officer) from the former Verification of Reintegration and Rural Reform Office to the Verification of Rural Reform Section; and (iii) 5 posts, comprising  two posts (1 D-1, 1 Local level) from the former Verification of Reintegration and Rural Reform Office, two posts (1 P-3, 1 Local level) from the Verification of Security Guarantees Section, and one post (1 National Professional Officer) from the Office of Chief of Staff, to the Front Office of Verification Division.

Reassignment: it is proposed to reassign one post of Special Assistant, Political Affairs (P-4) from the Office of the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General as Liaison Officer (P-4) in the Front Office of the Verification Division.

Realignment: it is proposed to realign the Regional Offices, Sub-offices, and Local Sites from the Office to the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General to the Verification Division to reinforce organizational coherence.

8.	United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH) performs a good offices and coordinating role, including in support of the constitutional and political process in Haiti, the promotion of accountability and respect for human rights as well as the rule of law. The mandate derives from Security Council resolution 2814 (2026), by which the Council revised and extended the mandate of the mission until 31 January 2027.

In its resolution 2814 (2026), the Security Council revised the mandate of BINUH to focus on: (a) Support the Haitian authorities on their efforts to organize and hold municipal, parliamentary and presidential elections and achieve a peaceful transfer of power to elected Haitian officials; (b) Coordinate international electoral assistance to Haiti in cooperation with other regional and international stakeholders; (c) Support Haitian authorities in efforts to reduce community violence, and assist in the design of a Haitian-led disarmament, dismantlement, and reintegration program; (d) Support Haitian authorities in addressing prolonged pretrial detention, provide  support to the Haitian judiciary in the monitoring of the functioning of the courts  and for its handling of high-risk individuals; and (d) monitor and report on cases of gang violence, criminal activities, and human rights abuses and violations, including sexual violence, as well as assist national authorities in strengthening respect for human rights.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the mission contributes, is to strengthen political stability and good governance, including accountability and the rule of law; restore a peaceful and stable environment; protect and promote human rights; and strengthen gender equality in Haiti.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, BINUH will:

Support the national authorities to advance and facilitate a Haitian-led, Haitian-owned political process aimed at reaching an urgent agreement on a road map for a peaceful handover of power following elections;

Support the Haitian authorities in efforts to reduce community violence and assist in the  design of a Haitian-led disarmament, dismantlement, and reintegration program including support for safe exit, voluntary disengagement, rehabilitation and reintegration pathways for individuals, particularly children associated with gangs, and the implementation of a handover protocol to ensure clear referral pathways to safely transfer children to child protection services;

Assist Haitian authorities in addressing prolonged pretrial detention through support to relevant Haitian institutions, and support the Haitian judiciary in its regular monitoring of the functioning of the courts, and providing support for its handling of high-risk individuals;

Monitor and report on cases of gang violence, criminal activities, and human rights abuses and violations, including sexual violence against all women, girls, men and boys, address sexual violence and assist national authorities in strengthening respect for human rights;

Cooperate with the Sanctions Committee established pursuant to resolution 2653 (2022) and its Panel of Experts in order to facilitate the Panel’s work and collaborate to assist the Haitian authorities, including the Anti-Corruption unit, in raising awareness of the reporting mechanism for the potential violations of sanctions, and urging implementation of the territorial arms embargo
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

Peaceful transfer of power with the installation of all elected officials and appointment of the Government cabinet of Ministers expected in 2027 following general elections currently scheduled for 2026;
The operationalization of a Haitian-led disarmament, dismantlement and reintegration programme in line with international standards;

The establishment of safe exit, voluntary disengagement, rehabilitation and reintegration pathways for individuals, particularly children associated with gangs in line with the handover protocol ensuring clear referral pathways to safely transfer children to child protection services;
A reduction in pre-trial detention and effective handling of high-risk individuals by the Government;
Improved protection responses, strengthened advocacy and increased national capacities to uphold and promote human rights, especially for women, girls, men and boys victims of sexual violence.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, BINUH collaborates with the Organization of American States (OAS), the Caribbean Community (CARICOM), the European Union (EU), the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) and international and national non-governmental organizations in Haiti. The mission also engages closely with the diplomatic community, as appropriate.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, BINUH works in an integrated manner with the UN country team under the umbrella of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for the period 2023-2027 and is supported by and coordinated with the United Nations Support Office in Haiti (UNSOH). BINUH also supports the in-country requirements of the Panel of Experts on Haiti.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

Political polarization is reduced as progress is made in the implementation of the political transition and toward the holding of elections, thereby strengthening the ability of national authorities to build the political consensus required to advance political, legal and judicial reforms;

The establishment and manning of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) supported by the United Nations Office for Support in Haiti (UNSOH) significantly improves the security situation, positively affecting both the pace and sustainability of the political process;

The mission integrates a gender perspective into its planning, operations, deliverables and results, as appropriate, and encourages the meaningful participation of women in political processes, dialogues and negotiations, as well as their representation in decision-making positions. In addition, the mission continued to work with civil society actors focusing on gender and human rights in the context of the implementation of recommendations issued by the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women in 2016 and the second universal periodic review cycle for Haiti on the human rights situation.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the programme to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
Programme performance in 2025
National police authorities improved police performance and enhanced security in Haiti

In 2025, BINUH provided daily strategic and operational advice to Haitian National Police (HNP) and the Penitentiary Administrative Directorate (DAP) on critical policing matters, including anti-gang and anti-kidnapping operations, intelligence, election security, judicial police, criminal investigations, weapons and ammunition management, gender equality, legal framework, and police integrity and oversight. Additional support was provided to the Command, Control, Communication and Intelligence Centre, the Directorate of the Strategic Planning and Development for the preparation of the next HNP Strategic Development Plan, a fundamental planning and operational guide which directs the development targets for the HNP on a 5 year horizon, accompanied by diagnostic forums and meetings with participation of HNP and international partners, as the first step toward formulating the new strategic plan.

In 2025, the mission supported and undertook advocacy, outreach, dialogue facilitation, technical advice, and good offices actions to advance the political and electoral processes, sustaining and supporting the complex political process in Haiti. The fragmentation of the political and social landscape, with more than 300 political parties officially registered, required BINUH to facilitate consultations in Port-au-Prince and Cap Haïtien, which brought together civil society organizations, political parties, and private sector representatives, including the participation of women and youth.

BINUH provided advice and guidance to the Haitian Provisional Electoral Council, specifically on the electoral legal framework and inclusion of women in the electoral process. In 2027, the mission will support Haitian authorities in the design of a Haitian-led disarmament, dismantlement, and reintegration (DDR) programme including support for safe exit, voluntary disengagement, rehabilitation and reintegration pathways for individuals, particularly children associated with gangs in line with the handover protocol signed between the Government of Haiti and the United Nations to ensure clear referral pathways to safely transfer children to child protection services.

In parallel, BINUH will also assist Haitian authorities in addressing prolonged pretrial detention through support to relevant Haitian institutions, monitoring the Courts, and supporting its handling of high-risk individuals.
Lessons learned and planned change

A key lesson learned from the severe security conditions in 2025 which required the evacuation of most international staff and significantly constrained operational capacity, is the need for greater operational flexibility. In applying this lesson, BINUH has designed operations to be more flexible, with strengthened business continuity arrangements, clear prioritization of core activities, realistic delivery modalities and enhanced coordination with the UN country team and partners to sustain engagement where possible.

The proposed resource requirements for 2027 for BINUH amount to $31,614,900 (net of staff assessment) and would provide for the deployment of 5 United Nations police officers ($307,200), salaries and related costs ($20,611,500) for the deployment of 69 international posts and positions (1 Under-Secretary-General, 1 D-2, 4 D-1, 9 P-5, 16 P-4, 4 P-3, and 34 Field Service) and 32 national posts and positions (19 National Professional Officer, 1 General Service (Other level) and 12 Local level) and 10 government-provided personnel, inclusive of the establishment of 11 new civilian positions comprising four general temporary assistance and 7 government-provided personnel positions; and operational costs ($10,696,200).
Staffing requirements

For 2027, the proposed staffing changes for BINUH were developed following the adoption of the resolutions 2793 (2025) and 2814 (2026), where the Council reviewed the mandate of the Office and the operational framework, as further detailed in table 66 above and table 67 below.
Mission support services provided by UNSOH

In line with the provisions of paragraph (e) of the resolution 2793 (2025), the Office proposed abolishment of the Mission Support Service and related posts, with the exception of seven posts identified for reassignment, following the assumption by UNSOH of responsibility for the delivery of standard range of mission support services to BINUH, effective 1 February 2026, on a cost recovery basis in support of mandate implementation. As a result, it is proposed to abolish 38 support posts and positions (1 D-1, 4 P-3, 2 P-2, 8 Field Service, 1 National professional Officer and 21 Local level) and 1 United Nations volunteer and to reassign 7 posts (1 P-5, 1 P-4, 1 P-3 and 4 Field Service). This includes the proposed reassignment of one support post to the Office of the Chief of Staff as Programme Management Officer to act as the operational interface between BINUH’s substantive components and UNSOH’s mission support services.
Dedicated Electoral Affairs Section

Pursuant to paragraph 2 (ii) and (iii) of Security Council resolution 2814 (2026), the Office proposes the establishment of a dedicated Electoral Affairs Section to ensure the effective implementation of the mission’s expanded electoral mandate. The Section would be constituted through the redeployment of existing elections-related staff (1 P-5, 1 P-4, 1 National Professional Officer and 1 Local level) from the Political Affairs and Good Governance Service. This would be supplemented by the establishment of four general temporary assistance positions (2 P-3, one National Professional Officer and one Local level). Security Council resolution 2814 (2026) tasks BINUH with supporting Haitian authorities in the organization and conduct of municipal, parliamentary, and presidential elections, initially scheduled for 2026 and expected to extend in part into 2027, through a credible and inclusive process, and with contributing to a peaceful transfer of power to democratically elected officials. In this context, and in view of the critical nature of the forthcoming electoral process, additional capacity is required to coordinate international electoral assistance in close cooperation with regional and international partners, including the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) and the Organization of American States (OAS).
Disarmament, Dismantlement, and Reintegration and Community Violence Reduction, Corrections and Rehabilitation Service

In accordance with paragraph 2 (iv) and (v) of Security Council resolution 2814 (2026), BINUH proposes the establishment of a Disarmament, Dismantlement, Reintegration and Community Violence Reduction (DDR/CVR), Corrections and Rehabilitation Service, comprising the DDR/CVR Section and a Corrections and Rehabilitation Section. The proposed Service would support Haitian authorities in reducing community violence and advancing a Haitian-led disarmament, dismantlement and reintegration programme consistent with Haiti’s national strategy. The Service would provide assistance in the design and implementation of safe exit, voluntary disengagement, rehabilitation, and reintegration pathways for individuals formerly associated with gangs, with particular attention to children. and in line with the handover protocol ensuring clear referral mechanisms for the safe transfer of children to child protection services, while also providing support to national authorities on the handling of high-risk individuals falling outside DDR pathways, and assistance to efforts aimed at reducing pre-trial detention.

Following the abolishment of the police-related mandate for BINUH, the Office proposed to abolish five posts (1 P-5, 1 P-4, 2 P-3 and 1 LL) previously dedicated to the implementation of that element of the mandate and to abolish the Police and the Corrections Service and to enforce the Office’s DDR/CVR and corrections mandate. In this regard, it is further proposed to reassign the post of United Nations Police Commissioner (D-1) as the Chief of the DDR/CVR, Corrections and Rehabilitation Service (D-1), and to redeploy the remaining five posts (1 P-5, 3 National Professional Officer and 1 Local level) to the Corrections and Rehabilitation Section. In parallel, the number of United Nations police officers deployed in BINUH would be reduced from 48 to 5, limited to liaison and advisory functions with the local authorities. The Office also proposes an increase of seven government-provided personnel to perform functions of corrections officers to. help (i) in the supervision and monitoring of individuals detained by the GSF and handed over to national authorities, and (ii) with Weapons and Ammunition Management (WAM).

To reinforce support to the Directorate of Prison Administration, the Office also proposes an increase of seven government-provided personnel as corrections personnel. Their expertise will ensure that the Directorate is equipped with the necessary tools and guidance to improve prison administration and operational effectiveness. The seconded Corrections Officers will bring specialized expertise in juvenile corrections management, thereby enhancing BINUH’s capacity to support the Haitian juvenile justice system in line with operational paragraph 4 of resolution 2814 (2026).

Based on the above, the DDR/CVR Section will be staffed through the redeployment of 6 posts (1 P-5, 1 P-4, 3 National professional Officers and 1 Local level) from the Political Affairs and Good Governance Service. The Corrections and Rehabilitation Section will be staffed through: (a) the redeployment of five posts (1 P-5, 3 National Professional Officers and 1 Local level) from the Police and the Corrections Service, to be abolished; (b) the redeployment of 1 post (1 P-3) from the Office the Chief of Staff; (c) the reassignment of the post of Special Assistant, Political Affairs from the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General as Corrections Officer (P-4).
Other enhanced substantive capacities

As availability of sufficient capacity in 2027 will be critical to meeting the Office’s mandated objectives, BINUH further proposes to strengthen senior leadership and substantive capacity through the reassignment of two posts comprising: (a) Chief of Section, Supply Chain (P-5) to Special Assistant, Political Affairs (P-5) in the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General to provide immediate strategic support to the Head of BINUH; (b) Finance and Budget Officer (P-3) to Human Rights Officer (P-3) in the Human Rights Service for collecting, managing, analysing, and reporting crime data, including information on gangs and self-defence groups.
Close protection services

Following the recent review of the Office’s security arrangements conducted by the Department of Safety and Security, it is proposed to reassign four support staff as Close Protection Officers (Field Service) to establish an additional four-member Close Protection team within the Close Protection Unit (CPU), in line with the most recent security risk assessment. This adjustment is intended to ensure the continuous safety and security of senior United Nations officials assessed as facing heightened security risks.
Continuation of general temporary assistance positions
The approved 2026 staffing table for BINUH includes four general temporary assistance positions. It is proposed that the positions be continued in 2027, comprising the following:
Office of the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Political

One Principal Human Rights Officer (D-1) in the Human Rights Service to respond to and address the human rights requirements set by the Security Council as reflected in the BINUH mandate, adopted in resolution 2814 (2026). Such a dedicated position, with specific human rights expertise, is important to facilitate trusted engagement at a high level with senior Haitian authorities, allowing for the provision of technical assistance and advice to the country’s national human rights institutions;
Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (backstopping support)

Two backstopping positions in the Haiti team of the Americas Division of the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, comprising one Senior Political Affairs Officer (P-5), and one Political Affairs Officer (P-4), who have been providing backstopping support to BINUH since 2019 and will remain critical to ensuring ongoing support and strategic advice and analysis to principals at Headquarters for decision-making with regard to BINUH. The core functions that they undertake are required throughout the lifespan of the mission, including its start-up, the duration of the implementation of its mandate and its closing.
