9.	United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mandate of the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) is defined in Security Council resolutions 1401 (2002), 1662 (2006) and 2626 (2022), and renewed by its subsequent resolutions, including most recently resolution 2818 (2026), by which the Council extended the mandate of the Mission until 17 June 2026.

As currently mandated by the Security Council, UNAMA will continue to promote peace and stability in Afghanistan, including by coordinating and facilitating enhanced cooperation and coherence in the financial resourcing and delivery of humanitarian and basic human needs assistance that support strengthened resilience; coordinating efforts with donors and other stakeholders to reduce risk and increase accountability, transparency and effectiveness in the use of aid; supporting efforts, including the provision of essential services and economic recovery, to create the conditions for self -reliance and stability for the Afghan population; assessing the explosive ordnance threat and coordinating mitigation measures to enable humanitarian and development initiatives; providing outreach and good offices to promote dialogue between Afghan stakeholders, the region and the international community to promote inclusive and responsive governance, and providing advice on inclusive national and local consultative mechanisms, and confidence-building measures; engaging with all stakeholders on the promotion and protection of human rights, including the rights of women and girls; supporting regional cooperation; and supporting existing mechanisms to improve the overall security situation in Afghanistan, including regional and international efforts to prevent and address the illicit trade in and destabilizing accumulation of small arms and light weapons and their diversion in Afghanistan and the region.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Mission contributes, is to create the conditions for peace and stability, with foundations established for the promotion of inclusive and responsive governance and functioning and accountable institutions, as well as a coherent and sustainable path towards the economic and social conditions for self-reliance.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Mission will:

Coordinate with international donors, organizations and partners in addressing the humanitarian and basic human needs of vulnerable Afghans. The Mission will partner with the United Nations country team to support economic development and increase donor confidence for greater basic human needs support, as emphasized in the independent assessment on Afghanistan requested by the Security Council in its resolution 2679 (2023), and to implement the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, with a focus on the objectives of the Pact for the Future, particularly with regard to climate financing, poverty alleviation and upholding the principles and values of the Charter of the United Nations. To that end, it will support resource mobilization to enable humanitarian efforts, essential services, the restoration of livelihoods, support to the private sector, economic development and mitigation of the dangers of explosive remnants of war. The Mission will engage with the de facto authorities and other stakeholders to facilitate the support of the United Nations, international financial institutions and other international and national partners to the socioeconomic recovery of Afghanistan;

Provide outreach and good offices, including by facilitating dialogue between Afghan political actors and stakeholders, regional stakeholders and the wider international community. The Mission will use its convening platforms at the national and subnational levels to facilitate engagement and cooperation between the de facto authorities, civil society, young people, communities, women-led organizations and other stakeholders on governance and policy issues, such as inclusion, participation and responsiveness to constituency concerns. It will maintain support for promoting the participation of women and minorities in all spheres. It will also continue to identify further entry points for engagement with the de facto authorities for the benefit of all Afghans, including through the United Nations-facilitated Comprehensive Approach under the Doha Process comprising the contours of a political roadmap (“Mosaic”) and thematic working groups. In addition, the United Nations and international partners will monitor, report on and conduct analysis relating to the political economy. The Mission will provide technical and analytical support to United Nations agencies and humanitarian partners and will continue to engage with civil society, the media, communities and counterpart institutions of the de facto authorities, in compliance with the sanctions set out in relevant Security Council resolutions related to anti-money-laundering and combating the counter-terrorism financing;

Advise stakeholders on and promote respect for the human rights of all in Afghanistan and accountability for human rights violation, including women and girls, children, detainees and the prevention of their torture and ill-treatment, human rights defenders and civic space; and other vulnerable groups. In addition, UNAMA will continue to integrate human rights and gender mainstreaming as cross-cutting issues in mandate implementation. The Mission will promote and support gender equality, the empowerment of women and girls, and the participation and leadership of women in public life and at all levels and stages of decision-making. It will also partner with the United Nations country team to promote the protection and fulfilment of the rights of women and girls and the implementation of Security Council resolution 1325 (2000) on women and peace and security, and successive resolutions on the matter;

Support peace and stability in Afghanistan through consultations and by utilizing its convening power for dialogues with political stakeholders. The Mission will use existing mechanisms to advance regional cooperation on economic development and security to help to foster a regional environment conducive to sustainable peace and stability. In addition, it will propose and support regional approaches to issues, such as the return and reintegration of refugees and internally displaced persons, combating illicit drugs and trafficking, addressing the illicit accumulation and trafficking of small arms and light weapons in Afghanistan and the region, and reducing the illegal economy and its impact. It will also coordinate explosive ordnance threat mitigation measures to enable the safe delivery of humanitarian and basic human needs initiatives;

Intensify its work to implement the United Nations Strategic Framework for Afghanistan, 2023–2025, which has been extended to 2027, by engaging with the de facto authorities, civil society and the media to facilitate the transition of society from conflict to peace and the removal of explosive remnants of war. The Mission will contribute to the goal of reduced dependency on aid, increasing United Nations assistance in critical sectors, such as banking, trade and economic reform. The Deputy Special Representative/Resident Coordinator/Humanitarian Coordinator will ensure a coherent approach to United Nations humanitarian and basic needs programming for the benefit of the Afghan people. The Mission will streamline the delivery, oversight and reporting of aid provided in Afghanistan, in alignment with the Strategic Framework and in coordination with the de facto authorities, civil society and international partners. It will also enhance collaboration on aid architecture and risk management practices.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

The advancement of dialogue involving the de facto authorities and other national stakeholders within and outside Afghanistan, as well as the international community, to improve the situation of Afghans, including through efforts aimed at improving the inclusiveness and responsiveness of governing entities, and to support the creation of conditions that could eventually lead to the reintegration of Afghanistan into the international community, in accordance with relevant Security Council resolutions;

Increased compliance by all parties with international humanitarian law and human rights obligations, with improved accountability for human rights violations and abuses, contributing to building confidence in such mechanisms and between the population and the de facto authorities;
Ongoing accurate reporting to the international community on the evolving situation in Afghanistan and its implications for international peace and security;

Sustained local, regional and international support to meet humanitarian and basic human needs and promote economic development, and to create an environment conducive to socioeconomic recovery in Afghanistan.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the Mission supports constructive dialogue between the relevant Afghan stakeholders, regional actors and the international community that is focused on the rights and socioeconomic progress of the Afghan people.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, UNAMA engages with the United Nations country team to strengthen the repositioning of the United Nations development system and to deliver more effectively and efficiently in line with the 2030 Agenda, the Pact for the Future, the Sustainable Development Goals and the humanitarian-development-peace nexus. The Mission and the United Nations country team collaborate closely on issues related to governance, the rule of law, human rights and gender, focusing on policy issues and good offices. Given the context in Afghanistan, the Mission’s work also supports the delivery of humanitarian response and meeting basic human needs through the delivery of essential services, livelihoods and community systems, in line with Inter-Agency Standing Committee recommendations. The Mission supports the removal of explosive ordnance, the delivery of risk education and the provision of victim assistance to enable humanitarian and basic human needs activities. It collaborates with various stakeholders to explore new aid approaches targeting economic promotion and recovery. It also leads the coordination of an overall risk management approach of the United Nations in Afghanistan, including mitigating the risk of aid diversion. It engages with the United Nations country team to enhance operational effectiveness through shared services and premises, generating $3.5 million efficiency gains for the Mission under the United Nations Business Operations Strategy, reducing operational footprints and redirecting resources to programme delivery. In addition, the Mission coordinates on specific issues with the United Nations Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia to provide good offices and expert advice on confidence-building measures in the region that contribute to stability in Afghanistan.
With regard to external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

The de facto authorities will remain in control of the territory of Afghanistan. However, political, security, human rights, legal, socioeconomic and humanitarian uncertainties will continue. The likely continuation and furthering of restrictive policies will present challenges for the full reintegration of Afghanistan into the international community;

The lack of international recognition, and, to an extent, domestic legitimacy of the de facto authorities due to questions about lack of representation and inclusion, the dissonance between their ideology and international norms and standards, the continued absence of a constitution, the promulgation of repressive decrees, especially those aimed at women and minority groups, and the continued restriction preventing United Nations national female personnel from accessing United Nations compounds, will pose significant challenges in engaging with domestic, regional and international stakeholders on the future of Afghanistan;

The security situation will remain uncertain, with the likelihood of continued attacks by Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant-Khorasan against the de facto authorities and the international presence, activities of anti-Taliban armed opposition groups and dynamics related to the presence of regional and international foreign terrorist fighters and their access to illicitly accumulated small arms and light weapons, with an impact on the Mission, as well as on development and humanitarian actors, in terms of access and physical security. The de facto authorities’ security emergency response and information sharing remain inconsistent and security support systems facilitating UNAMA operations remain significantly dependent on United Nations assistance;
Relations between Afghanistan and some of its neighbours will remain tense due to unresolved security issues, threats of terrorism, migration and water management issues;

Civilians, including those working as humanitarians and supporting basic human needs, will continue to face the threats of explosive ordnance, including those from improvised explosive devices and explosive remnants of war;

Enduring threats, such as terrorism, organized crime and illicit trafficking, including in narcotics, small arms and light weapons, and resource competition, will continue, with threats emerging from issues such as land rights and the disenfranchisement of minorities, population outflow, returnees, unemployment and the impact of evolving regional dynamics, as well as vulnerability to the adverse impact of climate change, ecological changes and natural disasters, which may heighten the risk of local conflicts over land, water and other resources;

The economy and human development will remain adversely affected by the continuing impact of non-recognition and donor sensitivities, the severe restrictions by the de facto authorities on female national staff working for the United Nations and non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and the limitations of the de facto authorities to reinvigorate the economy and reduce poverty, with the resumption of development funding depending on the de facto authorities meeting international norms, especially in relation to the protection of human rights, including for women and girls;

In a context where funding is diminishing and mobilizing additional resources is increasingly challenging, the United Nations is expected to demonstrate increased complementarities and efficiencies in humanitarian assistance and recovery support. This includes focusing on meeting basic human needs by maintaining essential services and preserving community systems;

As viable alternatives for large-scale legitimate financial transactions remain unavailable, the United Nations will continue to rely on and incur the costs associated with the cash importation facility of the Secretariat, managed at Headquarters.

The Mission integrates a gender perspective in its operational activities, deliverables and results. For example, in its engagement with the de facto authorities and political stakeholders, UNAMA continues its advocacy for the full, equal and meaningful participation of women in political processes at all levels. The Mission continues to support the implementation of Security Council resolutions 1325 (2000) and 2493 (2019), particularly on gender equality, the empowerment of women and girls and their human rights.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, UNAMA will implement its revised strategic plan, with a focus on: (a) increasing engagement with persons with disabilities through outreach projects; (b) advancing disability inclusion in strategic planning and management, and strengthening institutional capacity; (c) further improving physical and digital accessibility to provide an enabling work environment for an inclusive and diverse workforce; and (d) continuous staff capacity-building and learning on disability inclusion.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Evaluation activities
An evaluation of the Mission’s mandate implementation (2021-2024), completed by the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS) in 2025 has informed the proposed budget for 2027.

The results of the OIOS evaluation guided the development of the Mission Concept 2026-2027 and ongoing efforts to strengthen human rights monitoring and reporting, and to empower the Integrated Office within the Office of the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General (Resident Coordinator/Humanitarian Coordinator) and regional mechanisms to enhance integration, coordination and collaboration in mandate implementation. UNAMA plans to conduct an internal evaluation of its information management in 2027.
Programme performance in 2025
Afghans retain access to dialogue and coordinated assistance

In 2025, amid heightened human rights, political, civic and economic constraints, the Mission undertook efforts to maintain a space (even though limited) for dialogue among Afghan stakeholders and between them and UNAMA and the international community. Despite persistent restrictions on media freedoms, civic space and Afghans’ enjoyment of their human rights, most acutely affecting women, Afghans retained access to channels to express concerns and communicate priority needs, enabling their voices to inform discussions on the protection of human rights, including the rights of women and girls, and advocacy for a coherent socio-economic, political and policy agenda.

Through various engagement modalities facilitated by UNAMA, Afghan stakeholders conveyed the impacts of these constraints on rights, livelihoods, social cohesion and economic conditions. Their perspectives informed international advocacy and dialogue on the country’s political trajectory, including the implications of continued constraints for Afghanistan’s reintegration into the international system. In parallel, the High-Level Coordination Forum and the Technical Level Coordination Forum with de facto line ministries, facilitated by UNAMA, enabled an assessment of how the United Nations could complement the implementation of the Afghanistan National Development Strategy 2025-2030 adopted by the de facto authorities.

Based on the areas of common interest for targeted action identified by UNAMA, information gathered from Afghan stakeholders supported more coordinated responses to growing economic pressures, climate-related shocks and limitations on private sector activity. The Mission promoted joint engagement and tangible actions to address the challenges faced by the Afghan population through the Counternarcotics and Private Sector Working Groups under the Doha Process, improved the coherence and predictability of assistance, contributing to a shift from emergency relief toward basic human needs support.

Result 1: Advancement in the efforts by the international community and the de facto authorities toward the full reintegration of the Afghan State into the international community – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

The international community, the de facto authorities and relevant stakeholders engaged in more coherent and structured direct dialogue, shaping conditions for Afghanistan to advance its reintegration into the international community and meet its international obligations.

Increased direct engagement was undertaken through the United Nations-facilitated efforts of the Comprehensive Approach. The contours of a political roadmap (“Mosaic”) consolidated and identified feasible initial steps to address six key issues affecting prospects for reintegration, including inclusive governance and human rights. The Counternarcotics and Private Sector Working Groups focused on practical measures to address challenges facing the Afghan people. Technical engagement progressed on access to finance, women’s economic empowerment and trade facilitation in support of private sector development. Practical cooperation also expanded on counter-narcotics priorities, including financial and in-kind support for alternative livelihoods, technical dialogue on drug-related health issues and strengthened cross-border and regional engagement. Enhanced coordination and expert exchanges, including Afghan women, contributed to increased information-sharing, more coherent resource mobilization and sustainable support for the Afghan population, while fostering incremental confidence-building to sustain continued engagement.

children.text: Result 2: Strengthened economic and social resilience in Afghanistan – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, the United Nations country team mobilized $1.76 billion for basic human needs assistance to the people of Afghanistan. At least 26.2 million Afghans accessed health care services; 2.5 million Afghans benefited from short-term employment and improved livelihoods through cash-based interventions; 545,360 Afghans enrolled in and/or accessed informal and non-formal education services and training; 29,256 teachers were trained; 105 business associations and chambers strengthened, including women’s business associations; and 3,650 loans disbursed to Afghan private sector through financial institutions. These results were possible through the implementation of basic human needs programmatic activities under the United Nations Strategic Framework for Afghanistan, which the Mission supported through coordination of United Nations agencies and resource mobilization with donors.

The Mission will continue to strengthen basic human needs programming in support of Afghan community resilience through coordination and resource mobilization, while maintaining advocacy to continue resourcing critical humanitarian needs with Member States, donors and the de facto authorities as the main duty bearers of the Afghan people. Furthermore, it will continue dialogue with the de facto authorities to promote a more conducive regulatory and operational environment for the private sector and aid organizations.

children.text: Result 3: Strengthened human rights awareness
Proposed programme plan for 2027

Strengthening human rights awareness in Afghanistan is essential to protecting civilians, promoting respect for human rights and accountability for violations, and upholding the country’s international obligations. UNAMA contributes by gathering credible information, raising awareness of international human rights standards and recommending concrete measures to enhance the protection and fulfilment of the rights of all Afghans, including through thematic public reports and periodic updates on the situation in the country. These efforts help ensure that human rights concerns remain visible nationally and internationally.

The Mission will continue its engagement and advocacy through monitoring, verification and engagement with relevant actors to promote respect for the rights of all Afghans. This will support tangible improvements in specific cases, including harm mitigation, prevention of further violations and facilitation of corrective actions. The Mission will also continue supporting awareness-raising initiatives at the subnational level with the de facto authorities and other individuals.
Lessons learned and planned change

A lesson for the Mission was that traditional field‑based monitoring, while essential, cannot be the sole method for documenting and verifying violations in Afghanistan’s current context. Underreporting, fear of reprisals and shrinking civic space require UNAMA to adapt its methodologies through the safe use of locally available technology to keep its human rights work credible, comprehensive and safe for those engaging with the Mission. In applying the lesson, the Mission will diversify and strengthen its approaches to monitoring and verification where direct access is limited, and communities face heightened risks in sharing information.

Building on the momentum of the Secretary-General’s UN80 Initiative, the proposed budget reflects targeted efficiency measures through organizational optimization, functional streamlining and more efficient resource allocation. These measures include the redistribution of responsibilities, consolidation of functions, adjustments to internal workflows, leveraging of technologies and the reprofiling existing positions to address operational gaps. Collectively, these adjustments enable UNAMA to maintain mandate-critical functions while safeguarding the effective and efficient delivery of the Mission’s mandate.
Abolishment

For 2027, the Mission proposes the abolishment of 61 posts and positions (6 P-4, 2 P-3, 15 Field Service, 10 National Professional Officer and 28 Local level), across the three components, comprising 19 substantive posts, 24 security posts and 18 mission support posts. The proposed  abolishments are informed by a review of operational requirements, workload distribution and the optimization of support functions.

In the substantive component, the proposed 19 post abolishments reflect the Mission’s adaptation to a more restrictive operating environment, evolving mandate priorities and ongoing liquidity constraints. Certain civil affairs, coordination, political outreach and rule of law functions no longer constitute discrete requirements and are absorbed by other existing capacities. In addition, front office functions in the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General are consolidated, made possible by streamlined processes and enhanced use of digital tools. A similar approach is applied in Field Offices, reflecting the absorption of functions within existing capacity, ensuring continuity in mandate delivery while aligning staffing levels with current priorities for a more efficient use of limited resources.

In the Security Section, the proposed 24 abolishments result primarily from strengthened internal coordination, optimized supervisory arrangements and the redistribution of responsibilities. Further efficiencies are achieved through greater reliance on existing capacity within the United Nations common system in Afghanistan and the use of external trainers from other duty stations, as required, to meet security training needs. In this context, UNAMA proposes the abolishment of the Security Training Unit, comprising five posts (3 Field Service and 2 Local level).

In the mission support component, the proposed 18 abolishments reflect the further integration of functions and the outcome of an ongoing review of the support requirements to ensure alignment with operational needs in the context of a reduced client base and footprint, including the closure and nationalization of additional field offices in 2026.
Establishment
The Mission proposes the establishment of three international United Nations Volunteer positions comprising:
one position of Security Officer in the Security Section to monitor and coordinate guard force activities, support access control oversight, and undertake routine compliance follow-ups; and

two positions of Medical Officer, one each in Gardez and Kunduz Field Offices, costed at 30 per cent cost of the total cost of the two positions, with the remaining 70 per cent funded by the Joint Medical Services (JMS) participating entities, based on the cost-sharing arrangement in place under existing memoranda. The positions will provide on-site primary health care, respond to and stabilize medical emergencies within the compound and coordinate referrals to the regional hospital as needed.
Reclassification

In the Risk Management and Coordination Section, the Mission proposes the downward reclassification of two posts: One post of Chief of Risk Management and Compliance (P-5) to Chief of Risk Management and Compliance (P-4); and one post of Risk Management and Compliance Officer (P-4) to Risk Management and Compliance Officer (P-3). The proposed reclassifications reflect the stabilization of the Mission’s risk management architecture and the shift of the core functions towards sustained implementation, coordination, monitoring and incremental refinement of established frameworks, policies and tools.  The functions of the P-5 post have evolved towards sustained technical coordination and advisory support, which are more appropriately aligned with the P-4 level.  Consequent to this adjustment, the existing P-4 post is proposed for downward reclassification to the P-3 level.
Reassignment
Security Section
Within the Security Section, the Mission also proposes the reassignment of one post (Field Service) and one position (international United Nations Volunteer) as follows:

the reassignment of one post of Requisition Assistant (Field Service) as Administrative Assistant (Field Service), reflecting the evolution of functional requirements towards administrative coordination, controlled documentation handling, and workflow management in an integrated operating environment; and

the reassignment of one post of Political Affairs Officer (international United Nations Volunteer) from the Bamyan field office as Security Officer (international United Nations Volunteer), to undertake security risk management governance and oversight, operational security support, compliance monitoring, and security enabling services in support of personnel safety, movement, facilities, and programme delivery.
Redeployment

Within the Office of the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General (Resident Coordinator/ Humanitarian Coordinator), a need has been identified to strengthen the Mission’s capacity in the area of climate, peace and security, as well as to address the workload gaps at the national level.  Accordingly, it is proposed to redeploy one post of Political Affairs Officer (P-3)  from the Political Affairs Service one post of Assistant Programme Management Officer (National Professional Officer) from the Kandahar field office.
In line with operational requirements, it is also proposed to redeploy one post of Vehicle Technician (Local level) from the Transport Section to the Kandahar field office.

Three positions consisting of one Senior Programme Management Officer (P-4), Associate Programme Management Officer (National Professional Officer) and Data Analysis Assistant (Local level), funded under general temporary assistance, were established to support the mine action programme in UNAMA. The UNAMA Mine Action Unit supports the implementation of the Mission’s mine action programme in line with Security Council resolution 2626 (2022), paragraph 5 (c), last renewed in 2026; provides technical expertise and advice to Mission leadership and relevant stakeholders on mine action and engages with national mine action authorities, the United Nations country team and the humanitarian team to advocate for mine action. The decrease in requirements for 2027 compared with the appropriation for 2026 is attributable primarily to reduced requirements for civilian personnel costs, reflecting the proposed abolishment of 61 posts and positions (6 P-4, 2 P-3, 15 Field Service, 10 National Professional Officer and 28 Local level), the absence in 2027 of a one-time provision included in the 2026 appropriation for separation costs related to the abolishment of 38 posts in the Kuwait Joint Support Office, and the application of a higher vacancy rate of 13.4 per cent for international staff, compared with a vacancy rate of 10.4 per cent  applied in 2026. The decrease is further attributable to reduced operational cost requirements as detailed below.
A net decrease of $1,787,500 under operational costs is attributable mainly to the following changes:

Facilities and Infrastructure: The decrease in requirements of $1,014,200 reflects mainly lower fuel requirements for generators, estimated at 3.6 million litres at a weighted average price of $0.859, compared with 4.1 million litres at an average price of $0.853 included in the 2026 approved budget. The reduction reflects energy-efficiency measures and a reduced mission footprint following the closure and nationalization of field offices approved in 2026, as well as lower acquisition requirements based on projected stock levels at the end of 2026. The decrease is offset in part by additional requirements for the Mission’s cost-shared portion of shared security services at the Gardez and Kunduz field offices and rental costs for the Mazar field office, which had previously been provided free of charge.

Air operations: The decrease in requirements of $395,200 is attributable primarily to a decrease of 279 flight hours for the fixed-wing aircraft, from 686 to 407, based on the recent historical utilization patterns.

Communications and information technology: The decrease in requirements of $273,600 reflects primarily the removal of provisions for the Mission’s cost-shared portion for the Kuwait Joint Support Office and lower requirements for centralized services, owing to reduced unit costs and a smaller mission staff footprint.  The decrease is offset in part by additional requirements for software licencing to support the Mission’s Smart Camp infrastructure, as well as for the acquisitions of equipment for the upgrading of the security surveillance system and video conferencing units that no longer meet modern technical standards.

Ground transportation: The decrease in requirements of $134,700 is attributable primarily to the non-recurrent nature of the provision included in the 2026 approved budget for the acquisition of vehicle workshop equipment.

Medical: The decrease in requirements of $91,700 is attributable primarily to the lower costs for the critical care team (CCT) services under new contractual terms and operating modality. Under the former Forward Surgical Team (FST) and the Aeromedical Evacuation Team (AMET) arrangement, there was a standing Forward Surgical Team with embedded surgical capability, post-operative/ICU support and AMET services. Following a review of the utilization and operational needs, this was scaled down to the current CCT/AMET model, with personnel reduced from seven to three and the surgical capability demobilized.  Under the new modality, UNAMA retains a 24/7 emergency stabilization, critical care support and CASEVAC/MEDEVAC capability, surgical cases are stabilized by the CCT/AMET and referred to suitable local facilities or evacuated out of the country, if clinically required. The reduction reflects lowered number of personnel enabled by the shift from a standing surgical platform to a leaner stabilization-and-referral model.

Other supplies, services and equipment: The increased requirements of $121,900 are attributable primarily to additional requirements for mine detection and mine clearing services to strengthen mine action coordination, including support to the Mine Action Technical Cell in line with para 5(j) of Security Council resolution 2626 (2022). The proposed requirements would support the engagement of personnel including high-risk personnel, and operational costs through UNOPS. The increase in requirements is offset in part by reduced cash shipment fees following a downward revision of fee rates, reduced freight costs, and reduced requirements for rations based on revised contractual costs and reduced staffing levels.
Extrabudgetary resources
Voluntary contributions

In 2026, voluntary contributions in the amount of $2,130,995 are projected to be utilized under the Missions’ trust funds to provide for ten positions (1 P-5, 2 P-4, 6 P-3 and 1 Field Service), and operational costs to support climate change activities in local peace initiatives, political engagement and meetings with regional governments, and the advancement of international engagement on Afghanistan in a more coherent, coordinated, and structured manner in line with the recommendations of the Independent Assessment on Afghanistan (S/2023/856).

In 2027, voluntary contributions in the amount of $1,763,673 are projected to be utilized under the Missions’ trust funds to continue to provide for one P-4 position, and four P-3 positions for 6 months.
The decrease in the estimates projected for 2027 compared with the estimates of 2026 reflects the duration of the commitments made by the respective donors under existing agreements.
(b)	Cost recovery

In 2026, resources in the amount of $18,955,000 are estimated to be received from United Nations agencies, funds and programmes and other entities through the cost recovery mechanism, for services provided by the Mission, including co-location in Mission compounds and medical services throughout Afghanistan. These cost recovery resources will be utilized to provide for the staff costs of five positions (1 P-3 and 4 Field Service) and for medical-related requirements, including medical personnel and supplies, as well as the costs associated with maintaining United Nations compounds, including security services, rent, utilities and maintenance services. Such resources will complement regular budget resources of the Mission.

For 2027, resources in the amount of $18,955,000 are estimated to be received from United Nations agencies, funds and programmes and other entities. These estimates are based on existing clients and cost shared allocations and does not take into account any possible substantial reductions in the number, size and funding ability of the entities, which could translate to lower collections and higher cost-shared portion of costs for UNAMA and the other entities who would remain under the existing collocation arrangements.

Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions
(A/80/7/Add.13)

The Advisory Committee trusts that the Secretary-General will ensure the continued implementation of mandated activities and will address the challenges related to the proposed reduced level of resources. The Committee looks forward to receiving updated information on mandate implementation and comprehensive mitigation plans in the next budget submission. (para. 10).

UNOWAS reaffirms its commitment to ensuring the continued implementation of mandated activities despite the proposed reduced level of resources. The Mission will work to address related challenges and will provide updated information on mandate implementation, along with comprehensive mitigation measures, in the next budget submission.

UNRCCA takes note of the observations of the Advisory Committee and reiterates its commitment to ensuring the full and effective implementation of its mandated activities. Despite the challenges associated with the proposed reduction in resources, UNRCCA will make every effort to optimize the use of available capacities, prioritize critical areas of work, and maintain the delivery of key programmatic objectives. The Centre will also continue to assess operational risks and develop appropriate mitigation measures to minimize any potential impact on mandate implementation. UNRCCA stands ready to provide updated information on progress achieved and to present comprehensive mitigation plans in the context of the next budget submission, in line with the Committee’s request.

CNMC reaffirms its commitment to ensuring the continued implementation of mandated activities despite the proposed reduced level of resources. The Mission will work to address related challenges and will provide updated information on mandate implementation, along with comprehensive mitigation measures, in the next budget submission.

UNSCOL is committed to ensuring the uninterrupted implementation of its mandated activities. Every effort is being made to prioritize critical deliverables, enhance operational efficiency, and optimize the use of available resources, while maintaining the quality and timeliness of outputs. In this regard, measures are being developed and implemented to mitigate potential impacts. These include the reallocation of resources where feasible. The responsibilities of abolished posts have been redistributed among existing staff within the relevant units and sections.

UNOCA will scale back several of its programmatic activities in 2027 as a result of the reduced workforce following the UN 80 initiative and consequent revised budget. UNOCA workforce has reduced from 50 to 40 and majority of personnel cuts were in the substantive sections which had the highest number of personnel as well as vacant positions. This notwithstanding UNOCA will ensure effective mandate delivery through the use of virtual engagement, reduced travel, effective coordination with partners as well as use of in-house resources. UNOCA will adjust its operational model to deliver priority mandate tasks, including through workforce profiling, efficiency measures and greater reliance on partnerships with regional organizations.

The Advisory Committee acknowledges that the proposed posts and positions for the missions under thematic cluster III for 2026 represent a decrease in the proportion of P-5 and above posts and positions in the staffing complement from 7.87 per cent in 2025 to 7.79 per cent in 2026. The Committee also notes that the proportion of national posts compared with international posts would increase, from 46.24 per cent to 46.51 per cent. The Committee trusts that the Secretary-General will continue to holistically assess mission structures as well as the number and levels of posts, to ensure balanced staffing components, including though rejuvenation, by maintaining and recruiting lower-level staff, as well as by promoting the nationalization of posts and positions as appropriate, and that related proposals will be presented in the next budget submission. (para. 17).

UNOWAS and CNMC supports continued efforts to ensure balanced staffing structures, including rejuvenation through recruitment at lower levels and increased nationalization of posts where appropriate. UNOWAS will continue to assess its staffing needs holistically and reflect relevant proposals in its next budget submission.

UNRCCA remains committed to maintaining a balanced and effective workforce. The Centre will continue to review its structure holistically, supporting staff development at all levels and promoting the appropriate nationalization of posts. Relevant adjustments and updates will be reflected in future budget submissions.

UNSCOL strives to ensure balanced staffing across its components in terms of staff levels and the composition of international versus national personnel within the organizational structure. The Office continues to ensure that all functions are effectively and appropriately staffed and that operational priorities are met.

UNOCA already has a lean organizational structure of 50 posts which was reduced to 40 following the UN 80 initiatives and revised budget estimate reduction of 20% of UNOCA workforce. In order to meet the requirements of its mandate UNOCA has proposed in its 2027 budget submission to reclassify and redeploy 2 vacant international posts P level to section which has critical need.

UNVMC’s national staff complement exceeds that of international staff (51 per cent national staff posts versus 48 per cent international posts). Moreover, UNVMC is proposing the abolishment of a D-1 post and conversion of two international staff posts to national.

The Advisory Committee notes the intention of UNOWAS to thoroughly examine the current structure and trusts that more information in that regard will be provided to the General Assembly at the time of consideration of the present report and in the next budget submission (para. 27).

UNOWAS confirms its intention to thoroughly review its current structure. The Mission will provide further information to the General Assembly during its consideration of the present report and will include additional details in the next budget submission.

While acknowledging the operational requirements of the mission, in view of the scenario of constrained resources, the Advisory Committee trusts that UNOWAS, with guidance and support from United Nations Headquarters, will explore further options for a more cost-effective solution for travel, including further inter-mission cooperation or inter-agency cost-sharing arrangements for the aircraft, or standby charter options, for optimal use of resources. The Committee trusts that information in that regard will be provided in the next budget report. (para. 33)

UNOWAS takes note of the Advisory Committee’s observations in paragraph 33 and will continue to explore more cost effective travel solutions, in coordination with United Nations Headquarters. The Mission will assess options such as enhanced inter mission cooperation, inter agency cost sharing arrangements, and standby charter options to ensure optimal use of resources. Relevant updates will be reflected in the next budget report.

Taking into consideration the reduced footprint of UNOWAS, the Advisory Committee trusts that all efforts will be undertaken by the mission to review its vehicle fleet, and that options to cover surge requirements, including further cooperation with other entities from the United Nations system on the ground, will be further explored. The Committee trusts that information in that regard will be provided in the next budget report. (para.34.)

UNOWAS will continue reviewing and rationalizing its vehicle fleet in line with its reduced footprint. The Mission will also further explore options to meet surge requirements, including strengthened cooperation with other United Nations entities on the ground. Relevant updates will be reflected in the next budget report.

The Advisory Committee trusts that further information on the strategic review and the staffing review will be provided to the General Assembly at the time of its consideration of the present report and in the next budget submission. (para. 81)

Following the mandate renewal through resolution 2796 (2025) and the approval of the recommendations of the Strategic Review (S/2025/611), the Mission initiated a series of measures to translate these recommendations into operational, substantive and structural adjustments. Building on the outcomes of the Mission leadership retreat and subsequent implementation planning, UNSMIL has undertaken a broader strategic realignment to ensure that its substantive and operational activities directly support political outcomes and contribute to the implementation of the UNSMIL-facilitated political roadmap. Across the Mission, sections have reviewed and updated workplans, priorities and delivery frameworks to sharpen their focus on support to the political process, institutional unification and stabilization efforts. This has included the reorganization and redeployment of staffing capacities, refinement of reporting and coordination arrangements, and alignment of individual workplans and senior management compacts with the Mission’s central political objectives. Strategic planning instruments, including the Mission Concept, programme plans and resource proposals, have similarly been adjusted to ensure that activities and resources are directed toward advancing mandate implementation under constrained resource conditions. 

The Mission has already undergone significant structural adjustments, including the redeployment of 33 posts and positions to Tunis in the first quarter of this year and the abolition of 84 posts as part of broader resource optimization measures under the UN80 framework. While these measures have generated notable efficiencies, however these changes have created staffing constraints, altered the staffing profile and operating assumptions under which previous staffing assessments were conducted. In this context, a staffing review is required to ensure continued alignment between the Mission’s structure, operational requirements and mandate priorities, including the identification of emerging capacity needs and the adjustment of staffing configurations where necessary to sustain effective mandate delivery. This exercise is further aligned with the recommendations of the Strategic Review, which emphasize enhancing organizational efficiency, strengthening prioritization and ensuring that staffing capacities remain fit for purpose.

The Advisory Committee notes the proposed conversion of one vacant post of Translator (P-3) to Translator (National Professional Officer) to enhance the efforts of UNSMIL to build national capacity. The Committee trusts that UNSMIL will review its requirements for translators and propose additional conversions from the Professional level to the National Professional Officer level in the next budget submission. (para. 82).

The Mission takes note of the Advisory Committee’s observations regarding the translation function and the potential for further nationalization of capacities where operationally feasible. Within the context of the upcoming staffing review process, UNSMIL will continue to assess its capacity requirements, including within the translation unit, taking into account evolving operational needs, mandate implementation requirements and opportunities to strengthen national capacities. At present, however, the translation and interpretation functions remain critical at the proposed level given the sustained operational demands arising from the Mission’s support to the political process, including high-level political engagement, facilitation efforts and the ongoing Structured Dialogue framework. These activities require timely, accurate and high-quality translation direct support to facilitate engagement with national stakeholders, enhance dialogue processes and ensure effective communication across multiple tracks and levels of engagement. The Mission will continue to review its requirements within the broader staffing review exercise and will reflect any proposed adjustments, where justified by operational developments and mandate needs, in future budget submissions.
Action taken to implement the recommendation
Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (A/80/7/Add.14)

The Advisory Committee trusts that the Mission will provide an update on the recruitment status of all vacant posts and positions to the General Assembly at the time of its consideration of the present report and in the next budget submission. (para. 24).
As of 31 March 2026, UNAMA had 91 vacant posts and positions, of which 16 are proposed for abolishment. Information on vacant posts and positions is provided in the supplementary information.

The Advisory Committee, noting that the proposed abolishment’s coincide only in part with vacant posts, trusts that, where feasible, staff currently encumbering posts proposed for abolishment shall be reassigned to existing vacant posts, in order to retain institutional memory and ensure continuity of expertise, and looks forward to information in that regard being provided in the next budget submission. (para 26)

UNAMA has, to the extent possible, identified suitable positions for staff whose positions were abolished.  Positions were identified for 47 staff, whereas the Mission has not been able to identify suitable vacant positions for 32 staff members.

The Advisory Committee notes that the postponement of infrastructure projects represents a deferral rather than the elimination of the related requirements and trusts that the Mission will continue to monitor and plan for the eventual costs and potential safety implications arising from such delays and will provide the related updates to the General Assembly at the time of its consideration of the present report and in the next budget submission (para. 35).

No proposal is made in the 2027 proposed budget for these projects. UNAMA will rely on additional funding expected to be generated under cost recovery (10RCR) from the absorption of new agencies into the compounds, primarily Kabul Mission Headquarters (UNOCA), to complete works to improve the security and energy efficiency of existing buildings, as well as to create a central warehouse that will permit the consolidation of assets and consumables that are currently dispersed across multiple storage locations, for more efficient management of this material, while at the same time freeing up land for other agencies to collocate in the compounds, reducing the unit cost for all tenants.

The Advisory Committee trusts that the Secretary-General will ensure the continued implementation of mandated activities and address challenges related to the proposed level of resources. The Committee looks forward to receiving updated information on mandate implementation and comprehensive mitigation plans in the next budget submission. (para. 39)

To mitigate the effects of resource reductions, the Mission has adopted the following measures:

Strengthened regional hub model for field offices: The Mazar Field Office functions as a northern hub, with an expanded area of responsibility from four to six provinces, including Baghlan and Faryab. It is supported by redeployed posts from the two closed field offices and operational resources to sustain regular travel and engagement deemed essential for the continued coverage of the two provinces. 

Continuity of local engagement: Two staff members from each of the closing field offices were selected to fill newly established positions in the Mazar Field Office, preserving institutional knowledge, access and transition.

Alternative modalities: Increased use of virtual engagement complements reduced in-person presence, including for interaction with women and other key interlocutors.

Partnership arrangements: Collaboration and cost-sharing with UN partners will continue to support implementation of mandate-related activities in cross-cutting or complimentary areas of engagement. 

Climate Peace and Security capacity transition: The extra-budgetary-funded Climate Peace and Security Advisor, funded through 2027, will be supported by redeployed staff, enabling the practical transfer of knowledge and deeper familiarization with the function. Following the cessation of extra-budgetary funding, relevant tasks will be absorbed using existing resources and capabilities, reinforced by the technical expertise and related programmatic activities of UN partners.
